# The Final at a Glance

This course is the short version. It keeps only what the quizzes, the midterm and the lectures say is most likely on the final, ranked by how likely it is. The full course is still there when you need more depth on something.

## What you're walking into

- **Thu Dec 10, 10:45am to 12:45pm.** Two hours, on paper, closed book.
- **One double-sided handwritten 8.5x11 sheet** of notes.
- **Comprehensive.** Every lecture counts, and if your final beats your midterm, it replaces it.
- The review classes (Dec 1 and Dec 3) go through the toughest questions from Quizzes 6 to 10. The midterm review did the same with Quizzes 0 to 5, and the midterm then reused those question shapes heavily. Expect that again.
- **DP and greedy are quiz-style only**: T/F and multiple choice, no code to write.
- The midterm came in four variants built from flipped or isomorphic questions. Learn why an answer is right, not the answer itself.

## Predicted shape (about 100 points)

| Section | Count | Points |
|---|---|---|
| True/false, full of "always", "every", "even in the worst case" | 15-20 | ~30 |
| Multiple choice: traces, "which bucket", "array after partition", Big O | 12-15 | ~35 |
| Short answer: the tightest Big O plus one line of justification | 2-3 | ~10 |
| Code: 2 fill-in-the-blank + 2 written from scratch | 4 | ~25 |

From Quiz 6 on, every quiz's code question was **fill in the blanks inside a given skeleton** (the linear-probing insert, the merge, countLeaves). The from-scratch code is most likely an array or pointer function, a linked list function, a recursive function, or a BST function.

## Where the points are

About 55-60% should come from material after the midterm, since it has never been on an exam. Big O questions show up inside every chapter, not just Analysis.

| Chapter | Points | | Chapter | Points |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| OOD | 5 | | Searching and hashing | 12 |
| Arrays, pointers, memory | 8 | | Sorting | 12 |
| Analysis | 10 | | Trees and BSTs | 12 |
| Linked lists | 7 | | Heaps and heapsort | 9 |
| Recursion | 7 | | Graphs and Dijkstra | 9 |
| Stacks, queues | 5 | | DP and greedy | 4 |

## How to use this course

Each chapter covers that topic's predicted items, most likely first. Two kinds of lessons:

- **Concept lessons** teach one rule: why it holds, a worked trace, and the trap he sets for it. Then 2 to 5 questions in his style.
- **Write It lessons** are the functions you're most likely to write by hand. Fill in the C++, then **Submit** runs every check, including memory leaks and out-of-bounds access.

> [!tip]
> The exam has no compiler. After you pass a Write It lesson, write the function again on paper from memory. Whatever you miss goes on your notes sheet.

lessons.readme:
# Write It: Make the Brewers Virtual

The cafe now sells hot tea and cold brew. `doOrder` shouldn't care which brewer is plugged in. It should say "add tea" and have the right thing happen. One interface, many types: that's **polymorphism**.

A base-class pointer is allowed to point at a derived object. The question is whose method runs. For a normal method, the **pointer's** type decides, at compile time:

![without virtual the pointer type picks the function](courses/diagrams/be5110e3-6825-5df3-a950-93620046b7fd/plain.svg)

Put `virtual` on the base's method and the **object's** actual type decides, while the program runs. That's called **dynamic dispatch**:

![with virtual the object type picks the function](courses/diagrams/be5110e3-6825-5df3-a950-93620046b7fd/virtual.svg)

```cpp
class TeaBrewerImpl {
public:
    virtual ~TeaBrewerImpl() {}
    virtual void addTea(Drink& drink) { drink.tea_type = "House Tea"; }
};
```

- The same goes for calls through a base **reference**.
- If the object's class didn't override the method, the **nearest base version** runs.
- What matters is `virtual` **in the base**. A derived method with the same signature overrides it, with or without writing `virtual` again. The word `override` only asks the compiler to double-check, and the lecture code leaves it out.
- If you'll `delete` through a base pointer, the base **destructor must be virtual**. Otherwise it's undefined behavior, and usually the derived destructor is skipped.

## Assignment

Make the brewers polymorphic.

1. [ ] Make `TeaBrewerImpl`'s destructor and its `addTea` virtual.
2. [ ] In `ColdBrewTeaBrewerImpl`, override `addTea` to set `tea_type` to `"Cold Brew"`.
3. [ ] Leave `DecafTeaBrewerImpl` empty and watch which version it gets.

lessons.readme:
# Pure Virtual Makes It Abstract

Sometimes the base class has no sensible version of a method. There's no "shape in general" with an area. So you declare it **pure virtual** with `= 0`:

```cpp
class Shape {
public:
    virtual ~Shape() = default;
    virtual double area() const = 0;   // pure virtual: no body here
};
```

![an abstract brewer with three derived classes](courses/diagrams/70ee0de4-5143-5b33-a703-dd31c084f20c/tree.svg)

| | `virtual` | pure virtual (`= 0`) |
|---|---|---|
| body in the base | yes | no |
| derived classes | **may** override | **must** override, or stay abstract |
| makes the class abstract | no | **yes** |

A class with even one pure virtual function is **abstract**:

- You **can't create** an object of it: `Shape s;` and `new Shape()` don't compile.
- You **can** have pointers and references to it: `Shape* p = new Circle();` is the whole point.
- A derived class that doesn't override **every** inherited pure virtual function is abstract too, so it can't be created either.

The trap he sets: a statement that sounds generous, like "the derived class inherits a default from the base." A pure virtual function has no default to inherit.

lessons.title: Who Is Built First, Who Dies First
lessons.readme:
# Who Is Built First, Who Dies First

A derived object contains a whole base part, so the base part has to exist before the derived part can be built on top of it. Tearing down goes the other way.

- **Construction:** base constructor first, then the derived constructor.
- **Destruction:** derived destructor first, then the base destructor. Exactly the reverse.

```cpp
class A { public: A() { cout << "A"; }  ~A() { cout << "~A"; } };
class B : public A { public: B() { cout << "B"; }  ~B() { cout << "~B"; } };

int main() { B b; cout << "|"; }   // AB|~B~A
```

**When** destructors run:

- A local (stack) object dies at the **closing brace of its scope**. Locals in the same scope die in **reverse** order of creation.
- An object made with `new` dies only at **`delete`**. No `delete`, no destructor, ever.

![two cafes constructed and destroyed as their scopes end](courses/diagrams/733bb6c8-4f3b-58c8-8c14-09bd1e430438/life.svg)

The trap: a false "because." "The base destructor runs first because the base was built first" sounds logical and is backwards.

> [!tip]
> Write the output as you trace: constructors as each line runs, then at each `delete` and each `}` write the destructors in reverse.

questions.question: True or false: when a derived object is destroyed, the base destructor runs first, because the base part was built first.
True or false: two locals declared in the same block are destroyed in the same order they were constructed.

lessons.title: Write It: Speaker Constructor and Destructor
lessons.readme:
# Write It: Speaker Constructor and Destructor

A quiz favorite: you get a class with one private member and two empty boxes, "write the constructor" and "write the destructor." No starter signatures, so every character is yours. Here's the shape to memorize, for a class with a `double` member:

```cpp
class Kettle {
    double liters;
public:
    Kettle(double l) : liters(l) {}                                 // constructor
    ~Kettle() { std::cout << "Kettle cooled." << std::endl; }      // destructor
};
```

**The constructor**

- Its name is exactly the class name. No return type, not even `void`.
- The parameter's type matches the member it fills: a `double` member takes a `double` parameter, not an `int` (an `int` would chop `1.5` down to `1`).
- After the colon goes `member(parameter)`. It's the **member's** name there, not the class name, and no `=`: `liters(l)`, not `Kettle(liters = l)`.
- It still needs a body, even an empty one: `{}`.

**The destructor**

- It's `~` plus the class name, with **empty** parentheses: `~Kettle()`. No parameters, no return type.
- It has **no init list**. Only constructors get a colon list.
- "Prints" means `std::cout << ... << std::endl;`. A destructor can't `return` a value, and returning a string wouldn't print anything anyway.
- You never call it. It runs by itself when the object goes out of scope, or at `delete` for an object made with `new`.

> [!warning]
> Copy the message exactly, punctuation included. `"Kettle cooled."` and `"kettle cooled"` are different output.

## Assignment

1. [ ] Write `Speaker`'s constructor: it takes the volume as a `double` and sets `volume` in an init list.
2. [ ] Write the destructor: it prints `Speaker off.` followed by `std::endl`.

It won't compile until the constructor exists.

lessons.title: Is-A, Has-A and the Three Pillars
lessons.readme:
# Is-A, Has-A and the Three Pillars

Quiz 1 asked you to name the idea from a description. There are three pillars, and each one answers a different question.

| Pillar | What it means | Example |
|---|---|---|
| **Encapsulation** | bundle data with the functions that use it, behind a public interface; hide the rest | private members plus a setter that checks its input |
| **Inheritance** | a new class reuses an existing one: **is-a** | `class MobileCafe : public Cafe` |
| **Polymorphism** | one interface, and the **actual type** picks the behavior | a `Brewer*` that runs whichever `addTea` the object has |

Polymorphism has two flavors. **Dynamic** (run time) is virtual functions. **Static** (compile time) is overloading and templates. Reusing base members is inheritance, not polymorphism, and that swap is his favorite wrong option.

**Is-a vs has-a** picks between inheritance and composition:

![an is-a arrow to the base class and has-a arrows to the members](courses/diagrams/550505c3-2643-5438-b66b-7995a434a907/both.svg)

- A food truck **is a** cafe: inherit.
- A cafe **has a** tea brewer: make it a member. A menu that holds many drinks **has** drinks (a `vector<Drink>` member). A menu is not a kind of drink, so neither inherits from the other.

Access:

| In the base it's… | inside a derived class (public inheritance) |
|---|---|
| public | usable |
| protected | usable |
| private | **inherited** (it's part of the object), but **not accessible** |

# Practice Like the Exam: Object-Oriented Design (True/False)

His OOP quizzes test whether you know the exact rule, and the wording is built so a half-remembered rule sounds right. The shapes he reuses:

- **Swapped pair.** "The constructor runs when the object goes out of scope, while the destructor runs when it is created." Both halves name real things, traded. Check each half on its own: which one *must*, which one *may*, which one comes first.
- **True fact, wrong "because".** "Destructors run at the end of `main` because that's when the program exits." If the reason is wrong, the whole sentence is False, even when the first half is true.
- **"Always" with a hole.** "A derived class can always call every base-class member function." Look for the one case that breaks it (here: private members).
- **Plain rule, said plainly.** "A destructor takes no parameters." No twist means True. Don't invent a trap that isn't there.

The choice and code questions come next lesson.

lessons.title: Stack or Heap: Where It Lives
lessons.readme:
# Stack or Heap: Where It Lives

Midterm Problem 1 was T/F on this. Look at where each piece ends up:

```cpp
int main() {
    Room* r = new Room();   // r: stack.  the Room it points to: heap
    Room spare = *r;        // spare: stack (a copy)
    delete r;               // frees the heap Room. r itself is still on the stack
}
```

![r on the stack points to a Room on the heap; spare is a separate Room on the stack](courses/diagrams/f30f5024-bd36-5324-a3d9-a4debd984ba3/pic.svg)

The rule:

- Anything **declared in a function** is on the **stack**: locals, parameters, and pointer variables like `r`. It disappears when the function returns.
- The thing **`new` creates** is on the **heap**. `new` hands back its address. It stays alive after the function returns, until somebody calls **`delete`**.

So one line like `int* p = new int[5];` touches both: `p` is on the stack, and the five ints are on the heap.

The trap he sets: "the pointer is on the heap." A pointer is just a variable. If it's declared in a function, it's on the stack, no matter where it points.

True or false: memory from `new` stays allocated after the function that called `new` returns, until something deletes it.

answers: a, b and the n ints
b and the n ints it points at
Only the n ints b points at
questions.answer: Only the n ints b points at

lessons.title: Value, Pointer or Reference?
lessons.readme:
# Value, Pointer or Reference?

Whether a function can change the caller's variable depends only on how the parameter is passed.

| Parameter | What the function gets | Can it change the caller's variable? |
|---|---|---|
| `int a` | a copy of the value | no |
| `int& a` | another name for the caller's variable | yes |
| `int* a` | a copy of the address | yes, but only through `*a` |

The pointer row is where the trap is. The function's `a` is a **local copy of an address**. Assigning to `a` itself changes only that local copy. Assigning to `*a` changes the caller's int.

```cpp
void swapPointers(int* a, int* b) { int* t = a; a = b; b = t; }   // caller sees nothing
void swapValues(int* a, int* b)   { int t = *a; *a = *b; *b = t; } // caller's ints swap
```

![swap steps 1 and 2](courses/diagrams/9cad54e5-597c-5c26-83f6-6b68a106922b/a.svg)

![swap step 3 and the result](courses/diagrams/9cad54e5-597c-5c26-83f6-6b68a106922b/b.svg)

The second trap saves the **address** instead of the value:

```cpp
void swapBad(int* a, int* b) { int* t = a; *a = *b; *b = *t; }
```

`t` points at the same int as `a`, so once `*a = *b` runs the old value is gone. With 1 and 2 you get `2 2`.

> [!tip]
> Every assignment that does real work in a pointer swap has a `*` on the left. Draw a box per variable and an arrow per pointer, and change one box per line.

lessons.readme:
# Write It: Swap Two Ints Through Pointers

Two students want to trade rooms. The app keeps each student's room number in an `int`, and we want a function that swaps them **in the caller's variables**.

A pointer is how a function reaches back into the caller. Pass the addresses, and the function can write through them:

```cpp
int x = 214, y = 108;
swapPtr(&x, &y);     // afterward x is 108 and y is 214
```

Inside `swapPtr`, `a` and `b` are local pointer variables holding those two addresses. The swap needs a temporary to hold one **value** while the other is copied over:

![swap steps 1 and 2](courses/diagrams/9cad54e5-597c-5c26-83f6-6b68a106922b/a.svg)

![swap step 3 and the result](courses/diagrams/9cad54e5-597c-5c26-83f6-6b68a106922b/b.svg)

Read the pictures from left to right:

1. `int tmp = *a;` saves the value at `a` (214).
2. `*a = *b;` copies 108 into `x`.
3. `*b = tmp;` puts the saved 214 into `y`.

`a` and `b` never change; only the ints they point at do. When the function returns, its frame disappears, and the caller's `x` and `y` keep the new values.

## Assignment

This is the start of `rooms.h`, a small file of room helpers we'll keep adding to.

1. [ ] Complete `swapPtr(a, b)` so it swaps the two ints that `a` and `b` point at.

It should also work when `a` and `b` point at the same int (nothing changes then), and on elements of an array, like `swapPtr(&rooms[0], &rooms[1])`.

> [!warning]
> The mistakes that cost points on paper:
> - **Swapping the pointers instead of the values.** `int* t = a; a = b; b = t;` only trades the two local copies of the addresses. The caller's ints never change. Every assignment that does the work has a `*` on the left.
> - **A temp with no type, or the wrong one.** Write `int tmp = *a;`. Plain `tmp = *a;` doesn't compile, and `int* tmp = *a;` doesn't either.
> - **Saving the address, not the value.** `int* tmp = a;` compiles but gets overwritten by `*a = *b;`.

lessons.title: Spot the Leaking Line
lessons.readme:
# Spot the Leaking Line

Midterm Problem 10 gave you a few lines and asked which one leaks. A **leak** happens the moment you lose the **last pointer** to a heap block before deleting it. Nothing can ever free it after that.

Three ways to lose it:

- **Reassign** the only pointer: `p = new int[20];` or `p = q;` while `p` held the only pointer to a block.
- **Return** from a function without deleting what it allocated.
- **Overwrite** it with `nullptr`. Setting a pointer to null frees nothing.

Trace this one:

```cpp
void f() {
    int* p = new int[8];
    int* q = new int[3];
    int* r = p;       // copies the address only: r and p share the 8-int block
    q = p;            // the 3-int block just lost its last pointer: LEAK
    delete[] r;       // frees the 8-int block, once
}
```

![after q = p, nothing points at the 3-int block](courses/diagrams/42685868-f5b0-5aa5-a673-674351eca401/pic.svg)

`int* r = p;` makes a second **arrow**, not a second block, so the 8-int block is deleted exactly once, through either name.

Match the forms:

| Allocate with | Free with |
|---|---|
| `new T` | `delete p` |
| `new T[n]` | `delete[] p` |

Mixing them (`new int[5]` then `delete p`) is undefined behavior.

answers: It leaks, since a is never deleted
It deletes the same block twice
b needed its own new[] first
The block is freed exactly once
questions.answer: The block is freed exactly once

lessons.title: Dangling Pointers and Double Deletes
lessons.readme:
# Dangling Pointers and Double Deletes

A leak is memory nobody points at. A **dangling** pointer is the opposite: it points at memory that's already gone. Quiz 2 Q7 on this was called the toughest question.

**1. Using a pointer after `delete`.** `delete` frees the block but does **not** change the pointer. It still holds the old address.

```cpp
int* p = new int(5);
delete p;
cout << *p;     // BUG: p dangles
p = nullptr;    // the habit that helps: null it yourself
```

**2. Returning a pointer or reference to a local.** The local lives in the function's stack frame, which is gone the moment the function returns.

```cpp
const int& square(const int& i) {
    int res = i * i;
    return res;          // dangling reference: res dies here
}
```

![main holds a reference into square's frame, which no longer exists](courses/diagrams/e5abdbc3-8af2-5906-b791-6d699f8721cd/pic.svg)

It compiles (maybe with a warning), and it is **not a leak**: nothing was made with `new`. The memory is reclaimed too soon, not never. Returning **by value** is always safe.

**3. Shallow copy, then double delete.** A class holding `int* data` with a destructor that does `delete[] data` but no copy constructor of its own gets the default one, which copies the **pointer**:

![a and b both point at the same heap array](courses/diagrams/2d72f1ca-7fe7-566c-905c-d75399421d65/pic.svg)

Two objects, one array. Changing one changes the other, and at the end both destructors `delete[]` the same array. The fix is a **deep copy** constructor: allocate a new array and copy each element.

Which function is safe to call and use the result of?
answers: int f() { int x = 5; return x; }
const int& f(int x) { return x; }
int& f() { int x = 5; return x; }
questions.answer: int f() { int x = 5; return x; }

answers: Each destructor frees its own array
Only a is destroyed, so b leaks

lessons.title: Write It: Is the Value in the Array?
lessons.readme:
# Write It: Is the Value in the Array?

A student asks: "is room 412 still on the open list?" The open rooms are in a C-style array, so we check them one by one. This is **linear search**, and quizzes ask you to write it from scratch:

```cpp
bool hasRoom(const int rooms[], int len, int room) {
    for (int i = 0; i < len; i++) {
        if (rooms[i] == room) return true;   // found it: stop right away
    }
    return false;                            // checked every one: it isn't there
}
```

The shape is the whole lesson. `return true` sits **inside** the loop, the moment you find a match. `return false` sits **after** the loop, because you only know the answer is "no" once you've looked at every element.

> [!warning]
> The mistakes graders take points for:
> - **`return false` in an `else` inside the loop.** Then the function gives up after looking at `rooms[0]` alone. `{3, 8}` searched for 8 returns false. Never decide "not found" inside the loop.
> - **No `return false` at all.** Falling off the end of a `bool` function is undefined behavior.
> - **Wrong bounds.** Use `i = 0` and `i < len`. `i < len - 1` skips the last element, and `i <= len` reads past the end.
> - **Asking the array for its length.** A C-style array has no `.size()` or `.length`, and inside the function it's only a pointer. Use the `len` parameter.
> - **A flag declared inside the loop.** If you track `bool found`, declare it **before** the loop. A variable declared inside the loop's braces is gone after the loop.

The worst case is that the room isn't there: all `len` elements are checked, so linear search is O(n).

## Assignment

1. [ ] Complete `hasRoom(rooms, len, room)`: return `true` if `room` is among the first `len` elements of `rooms`, and `false` otherwise.

# Practice Like the Exam: Arrays, Pointers and Memory (True/False)

His pointer questions are short and every word counts. The shapes he reuses:

- **Swapped pair.** "A pointer must be set when it is declared, while a reference can be left unset." Real rules, traded. Say each half alone: which one has to be initialized, which one can be reseated?

# Doubling Counters: Add the Rows

Midterm Problem 12, and it fooled almost everyone:

```cpp
for (int i = 1; i <= n; i *= 2)
    for (int j = 0; j < i; j++)
        work();
```

The tempting answer: the outer loop runs log n times, the inner "up to n," so O(n log n). **Wrong.** The inner loop runs **i** times, and i is small most of the time. Add the rows:

![bars of 1, 2, 4, 8, 16 adding to 31](courses/diagrams/93e2e892-483a-560b-b2a4-abe6d04a9bc8/trap.svg)

1 + 2 + 4 + … + n. With n = 2ᵏ, the geometric series gives 2ᵏ⁺¹ − 1 = **2n − 1** calls. That's **O(n)**.

Change the inner bound to `j < n` and every row is full:

![five bars of 16 adding to 80](courses/diagrams/93e2e892-483a-560b-b2a4-abe6d04a9bc8/full.svg)

Now it really is n · (log₂ n + 1): **O(n log n)**.

The same sum shows up when the counter **halves**: `for (i = n; i >= 1; i /= 2) for (j = 0; j < i; j++)` runs n + n/2 + … + 1 = 2n − 1 times. Still O(n).

**The justification he wants**, in one line: "i takes 1, 2, 4, …, 2ᵏ with k = log₂ n, so work() runs 1 + 2 + … + 2ᵏ = 2ᵏ⁺¹ − 1 = 2n − 1 times: O(n)."

questions.question: True or false: the loop above is O(n log n), because the outer loop runs log n times and the inner loop runs up to n times.

# Exact Counts in Nested Loops

Quiz 3 Q6, the lowest-scored quiz item, asked for an exact count, not just Big O. There are two cases.

**The inner bound doesn't use i: multiply.** `for i < n` around `for j < n/2` runs n · n/2 = **n²/2** times:

![six by six grid with the first three columns highlighted in every row](courses/diagrams/fdc166f5-578f-5dcb-b171-d6b0cbfcbd8a/half.svg)

A **constant** inner bound like `j < 20` is just a constant: n · 20 is O(n), not O(n²).

**The inner bound uses i: make a table and add the column.** The every-pair loop:

```cpp
for (int i = 0; i < n; i++)
    for (int j = i + 1; j < n; j++)
        compare(a[i], a[j]);
```

| i | 0 | 1 | 2 | … | n − 1 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| inner runs | n − 1 | n − 2 | n − 3 | … | 0 |

![six by six grid with the cells below the diagonal highlighted](courses/diagrams/db6e65b2-0976-5d0d-a0fc-d455153dc271/pairs.svg)

(n − 1) + (n − 2) + … + 0 = **n(n − 1)/2**. That's O(n²). With n = 5, it's 10 pairs.

Bigger inner counts give bigger sums. With `j < i * i` the rows are 0, 1, 4, 9, …, (n − 1)², which adds to about n³/3: **O(n³)** from just two loops.

![bars of length 0, 1, 4, 9, 16, 25](courses/diagrams/8d53207e-538d-5d88-a308-be067ad8efff/squares.svg)

**More than one input: keep the letters.** A grid of m rows and n columns where each cell scans its whole row does m · n cells × n per scan = **O(mn²)** (midterm Problem 11). Don't merge m and n into one letter.

> [!note]
> Note sheet: 1 + 2 + … + n = n(n + 1)/2, and 1 + 2 + 4 + … + 2ᵏ = 2ᵏ⁺¹ − 1.

# Costs Hidden Inside a Call

A call costs whatever **its** Big O is. Midterm Problem 14 hid an O(n) call in a loop condition.

```cpp
for (int i = 0; i < list.size() / 2; i++) {
    // O(1) work
}
```

The loop runs n/2 times. **If** `size()` walks the linked list to count nodes (the problem will say so), it costs O(n), and the condition calls it on **every** pass: n/2 · O(n) = **O(n²)**. If the list keeps a counter, `size()` is O(1) and the loop is O(n).

Other hidden costs he uses:

- **Comparing strings** costs O(length), not O(1). Searching n names of length up to L with `==` is **O(n · L)**.
- **Passing a container by value** copies all n elements: O(n) time and space before the function does anything. Pass `const&` when you only read it.
- **Library calls**: `std::sort` is O(n log n). Inside a loop of m passes, that multiplies.
- **Time and space are separate answers.** A double loop over pairs is O(n²) time but O(1) extra space.

True or false: if a linked list keeps a node counter, calling `size()` in the loop condition adds no extra Big O cost.
`void report(vector<int> v)` only reads `v`, and profiling shows each call spends O(n) before the loop starts. Which change fixes that most directly?

lessons.readme:
# Scaling and Loose Bounds

Three T/F favorites.

**1. Predicting time from the growth rate.** Grow the input by a factor k and plug it in:

| Function | n → 2n | n → 3n |
|---|---|---|
| n | × 2 | × 3 |
| n² | × 4 | × 9 |
| n³ | × 8 | × 27 |
| 2ⁿ | doubles every time n grows by **just 1** | |

Example: an O(n²) report takes 5 s on 2,000 students. On 8,000, n grew 4 times, so time grows 4² = 16 times: about 80 s.

**2. Big O is only a ceiling.** "f is O(g)" means f grows **no faster** than g. So if f is O(n), it's also O(n²) and O(2ⁿ). Those are **loose** but **true**. On a "which is false?" question, look for the one where f really grows faster than g, like "n² is O(n log n)." When a question asks for *the* run time, give the tight bound: the smallest, simplest class.

**3. Big O ignores constants, real time doesn't.** Insertion sort (about n²/4 steps) beats merge sort (about 2n log n steps) on small lists. So "O(n log n) is always faster than O(n²)" is **false**. It's faster for large enough n.

True or false: if f(n) is O(n), then f(n) is also O(n²).
True or false: an O(n log n) algorithm runs faster than an O(n²) algorithm for every input size.
Which statement is **false**?
An O(2ⁿ) algorithm takes time t at n = 20. About how long at n = 21?

lessons.title: Linked List Costs on One Table
lessons.readme:
# Linked List Costs on One Table

Every linked list cost question comes down to one fact: a node only knows the node **after** it. To reach anything else you walk from `head`, one node per step.

```cpp
struct Node {
    int elt;
    Node* next;   // nullptr at the end
};
```

![an array next to a linked list whose nodes sit at scattered addresses](courses/diagrams/233e412b-2d8e-5cdd-aac7-dac71095bbf0/array.svg)

From that one fact you can rebuild the whole table instead of memorizing it:

| Operation | Array list | Singly, head only | Singly, head + tail | Doubly, head + tail |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| insertFront / removeFront | O(n) shift | O(1) | O(1) | O(1) |
| insertBack | O(1) | O(n) walk | O(1) | O(1) |
| removeBack | O(1) | O(n) | **O(n)** | O(1) |
| retrieveAt / insertAt / removeAt(pos) | O(1) / O(n) / O(n) | O(n) | O(n) | O(n) |
| insertAfter a node you hold | O(n) shift | O(1) | O(1) | O(1) |
| clear() | O(1) | O(n) | O(n) | O(n) |

**Why removeBack stays O(n) with a tail.** `tail` finds the last node instantly, but removing it means changing the node **before** it: that node's `next` must become `nullptr`, and `tail` must move to it. Nothing points backward, so you walk from `head` to find it. A doubly linked list fixes this with `prev`.

**Why insertAfter is O(1).** If you already hold `p`, there's no walk at all:

```cpp
p->next = new Node{v, p->next};
```

**Why position ops are O(n) even doubly linked.** Knowing an index isn't holding a pointer. `insertAt(pos)` walks to the spot first; linking the node in is the cheap part.

> [!warning]
> He changes one word in the setup and the answer flips. Underline "with a tail pointer", "doubly linked", and "you already have a pointer to the node" before you answer.

True or false: you hold a pointer `p` to a node in the middle of a singly linked list. Inserting a new node right after `p` is O(1).
A singly linked list keeps **only** `head`. Which operation is O(1)?
A music queue removes songs from the back all the time. It's a singly linked list with `head` and `tail`, and `removeBack` is slow. Which change fixes this most directly?
answers: Make it doubly linked, with a prev pointer in each node
Move tail to the second-to-last node
Keep a count of the nodes in the list
Check for nullptr before every walk
questions.answer: Make it doubly linked, with a prev pointer in each node

lessons.readme:
# Read Before You Delete

Most linked list bugs on his exams are one of two kinds: touching a node after it's freed, or walking the list with the wrong loop.

## Grab what you need, then delete

Removing the first node takes three steps, and the order is the lesson:

1. `Node* tmp = head;` save the old front
2. `head = head->next;` move past it
3. `delete tmp;` free it

![removeFront: save tmp, move head, delete tmp](courses/diagrams/eca44f54-96d1-5db1-827f-96c15e9e8ef7/steps.svg)

The wrong orders each fail differently:

- `head = head->next;` alone never deletes the old front. Nothing points to it, so it **leaks**.
- `delete head; head = head->next;` reads `next` from a freed node: **use-after-free**. It may run today and crash tomorrow.
- `head = head->next; delete head;` deletes the node you meant to keep.

A one-node list needs no special case: `head->next` is `nullptr`, so `head` becomes `nullptr`. An **empty** list does, because `head->next` dereferences `nullptr`.

A destructor (or `clear`) is the same rule in a loop: save `next`, then delete.

![clear: save next, delete head, move on](courses/diagrams/ba9d93dd-e56e-52f3-97b7-c33fbcb23a63/steps.svg)

## Walk with `p != nullptr`

```cpp
bool findValue(Node* head, int val) {
    for (Node* p = head; p != nullptr; p = p->next) {
        if (p->elt == val) return true;
    } // end for
    return false;
}
```

The Quiz 4 rubric took points off for each of these:

- `p->next != nullptr` as the condition. It stops **before** the last node and crashes on an empty list.
- `return false` inside the loop. Then only the first node is ever checked.
- comparing `p == val` instead of `p->elt == val`.

questions.question: Which `removeFront` body is correct for a non-empty list?
answers: `Node* t = head; head = head->next; delete t;`
`Node* t = head; delete t; head = head->next;`
questions.answer: `Node* t = head; head = head->next; delete t;`

answers: It leaks the last node of the list
It never deletes the first node
It must use delete[] for each node
It reads cur->next after cur is freed
questions.answer: It reads cur->next after cur is freed

questions.question: True or false: with the loop condition `p->next != nullptr`, `findValue` still finds a value stored in the last node, because the body runs once for every node.
True or false: `removeFront` needs a special case for a one-node list, because `head->next` is `nullptr` there.

# Write It: Length and Contains

First question from the club: how many cards are in the deck? A linked list has no `.size()` to ask. The only way to learn anything about it is to **walk** it, node by node.

The pattern is a `for` loop with a pointer called `cur`:

```cpp
for (Node* cur = head; cur != nullptr; cur = cur->next) {
    // use cur->elt
}
```

`cur` starts at the first node, and `cur = cur->next` hops to the next one. When it falls off the end, `cur` is `nullptr` and the loop stops. Here's a count of a three-card deck:

![cur walks a three-node list and stops at nullptr](courses/diagrams/248da275-d60a-54e0-bf35-8683a1155840/walk.svg)

Two details make this pattern safe:

- `cur` is a **copy** of `head`. Moving it doesn't move `head`, so the list is unchanged afterward.
- If the list is empty, `head` is `nullptr` and the loop runs zero times. The empty case is handled for free.

Searching works the same way: walk, and stop early as soon as you find what you want. Quiz 4 asked for exactly this, written by hand, under the name `findValue`. The grading rubric took points off for each of these, so check your paper version against the list:

> [!warning]
> - The loop condition is `ptr != nullptr`, not `ptr->next != nullptr` (that skips the last node, and crashes on an empty list).
> - Test the **pointer**, not `*ptr`, and declare it as `Node*`, not `Node`.
> - Compare the **data**: `ptr->elt == val`, never `ptr == val`.
> - The loop must be able to end when `val` isn't there. A `while (true)` with no `nullptr` check never does.
> - `return true` goes inside the loop when you find it; `return false` goes **after** the loop, once every node has been checked. A `return false` inside the loop stops after the first node.
> - The return type is `bool`.

> [!tip]
> On paper, test every list function on three lists: empty, one node, and a few nodes. Most linked list bugs live in the first two.

## Assignment

We'll build the club's deck as a singly linked list of card numbers in `list.h`.

1. [ ] Complete `length(head)`: return the number of nodes. An empty list has length 0.
2. [ ] Complete `contains(head, v)`: return `true` if some node's `elt` is `v`, `false` otherwise.

Neither function should change the list.

# Write It: Remove Every Other Node

Here's a pointer manipulation problem from the midterm: thin the deck by removing every **second** card. Keep the 1st, 3rd, 5th, and so on, and delete the rest.

Use `head` itself as the walking pointer. At each kept node:

1. Save the node to remove: `toDelete = head->next`.
2. Link around it: `head->next = toDelete->next`.
3. Free it: `delete toDelete`.
4. Step to the next node to keep: `head = head->next`.

![removing every other node from 1 2 3 4 5](courses/diagrams/5604444a-1284-5fed-ae68-16297358037f/steps.svg)

The loop runs while **both** `head` and `head->next` exist. If `head` is null, we've run off the end. If `head->next` is null, `head` is the last node and there's nothing after it to remove.

The function takes `Node* head` by value, and that's fine here. The first node is always kept, so the caller's `head` never changes; walking the local copy can't hurt it.

Step 2 comes before step 3 for the usual reason: `toDelete->next` has to be read while `toDelete` still exists.

## Assignment

1. [ ] Complete `removeEveryOther(head)`: keep the 1st, 3rd, 5th... nodes, and `delete` every node you remove. An empty or one-node list is left as is.

# Write It: K-th From the End in One Pass

A card trick needs the k-th card from the **bottom** of the deck. One way: walk the list once to count its length n, then walk again n − k steps. That's two passes.

The midterm worksheet asked for it in **one pass**, with a hint: think about using two pointers.

The idea is to keep a fixed **gap** between two pointers:

1. Start `lead` and `trail` at `head`.
2. Move `lead` forward k steps. Now it's k nodes ahead of `trail`.
3. Move both one step at a time until `lead` is `nullptr`.
4. `lead` has fallen off the end, and `trail` is still k nodes behind it: exactly the k-th node from the end.

Here's k = 2 on `1 → 2 → 3 → 4`:

![lead starts k ahead of trail; when lead falls off, trail is k from the end](courses/diagrams/de93f8f0-b486-5ac2-a28a-1b281cc55a21/trace.svg)

```
k = 2:   1 → 2 → 3 → 4 → null
         T       L                 start: lead is k = 2 ahead
             T       L             move both one step
                 T       L         lead == null, stop → trail->elt == 3
```

Check the ends: k = 1 means `lead` starts one ahead, so `trail` stops on the last node. k = n means `lead` is already `nullptr` after step 2, so `trail` never moves and returns the first node.

Two pointers walking the same list like this is what lecture calls **pointer chasing**.

## Assignment

These go in `tricks.h`. None of them may change the list.

1. [ ] Complete `kthFromEnd(head, k)` in **one pass** with two pointers. k = 1 is the last element. Assume 1 ≤ k ≤ the length of the list.

# Write It: Reverse a List in Place

Lab 4's bonus task: reverse the deck **in place**, with these rules:

1. A single pass.
2. No recursion.
3. Constant space: no array or stack of nodes, and fewer than 5 pointers.

The trick is to flip every `next` pointer to point **backward**, one node at a time. Three pointers do it:

- `prev`: the part already reversed (it starts as `nullptr`, an empty list)
- `cur`: the node being flipped
- `nxt`: the rest of the list, saved before `cur->next` is overwritten

Each step: save `nxt = cur->next`, point `cur->next` back at `prev`, then advance `prev = cur` and `cur = nxt`.

![reversing 1 2 3: the prev list grows as the cur list shrinks](courses/diagrams/3ab2b9c9-a89f-5b8b-afbb-82f8f8437037/steps.svg)

```
start    prev → null                  cur → 1 → 2 → 3 → null
step 1   prev → 1 → null              cur → 2 → 3 → null
step 2   prev → 2 → 1 → null          cur → 3 → null
step 3   prev → 3 → 2 → 1 → null      cur → null, so return prev
```

The order inside the loop matters for the same reason as `removeFront`: once you overwrite `cur->next`, the rest of the list is unreachable unless you saved it in `nxt` first.

At the end, `cur` is `nullptr` and `prev` is the old last node, which is the new head. In Lab 4 that went back into the deck with `deck.setHead(lastNode)`.

lessons.readme:
# Base Cases That Get Skipped

A recursive function stops only if **every** path of calls lands on a base case. Having a base case isn't enough; it has to be reachable from every input you allow.

```cpp
int count(int n) {
    if (n == 0) return 0;
    return 1 + count(n - 2);    // count(3) -> count(1) -> count(-1) -> ...
}
```

Even n works. Odd n steps right over 0 and keeps going. Each call adds a frame to the call stack, the stack is finite, and the program dies with a **stack overflow**.

The same trap with a different step: `g(n - 3)` with base case `n == 0` only returns for multiples of 3. And with base case `n == 1`, `f(0)` calls `f(-1)` and never stops.

**How to check on paper:** trace the smallest few inputs by hand (0, 1, 2, 3). If one of them skips the base case, you've found the bug.

**The usual fixes:**

- widen the base case so nothing can step past it: `if (n <= 0) return 0;`
- check invalid input **before** recursing, the way Lab 5's factorial returns -1 for negative n

> [!warning]
> He likes "true or false: this function has a base case, so it always terminates." Having one is not the same as reaching it.

questions.question: True or false: a recursive function that has a base case can never overflow the stack.
True or false: `int f(int n) { if (n == 1) return 1; return n * f(n - 1); }` returns a value for every n ≥ 0.

answers: Add a second base case `if (n == 2) return 1;`
Change the base case to `if (n <= 0) return 0;`
Pass `n` by reference instead of by value
questions.answer: Change the base case to `if (n <= 0) return 0;`

Frames pile up until the call stack overflows

# Trace It with Brackets

To find what a recursive function returns, write each call as a frame in **brackets**, expand until you hit a base case, then collapse from the inside out.

```cpp
int mystery(int n) {
    if (n <= 1) return n;
    return n + mystery(n - 2);
}
```

```
mystery(5)
-> [5 + mystery(3)]
-> [5 + [3 + mystery(1)]]
-> [5 + [3 + [1]]]          base case returns 1
-> [5 + 4]
-> 9
```

When a function makes **two** calls, compute small values bottom-up instead of expanding the whole tree: f(0), f(1), f(2), ... until you reach the one asked for.

**Order of work decides output.** Code before the recursive call runs on the way **down**; code after it runs on the way **back up**, newest frame first. That's how `printReverse` prints a list backward:

```cpp
void printReverse(Node* head) {
    if (head == nullptr) return;
    printReverse(head->next);    // everything after me first
    cout << head->elt << " ";    // then me
}
```

![printReverse call frames and the order of prints](courses/diagrams/509e3d7b-7b95-5b2e-a096-7302f7681fb8/frames.svg)

**Stack space is the depth.** While the deepest call runs, every frame above it is still waiting. One call per node of an n-node list means n frames at once: **O(n) memory**, even with no `new` anywhere.

lessons.readme:
# Recursion Big O: Calls and Depth

For a recursion you haven't seen, ask two questions: **how many calls does each call make**, and **how deep does it go**?

| Function | calls per call | depth | time |
|---|---|---|---|
| `power_rec`, `sumDigits`, `countNodes` | 1 | n | O(n) |
| fast `power` (halves n) | 1 | log₂ n | O(log n) |
| naive Fibonacci | 2 | n | O(2ⁿ) |
| three calls on n − 1 | 3 | n | O(3ⁿ) |

Write the justification the way the midterm's model answer did: "Each call makes two recursive calls and n drops by one per call, so the depth is n and the runtime is O(2ⁿ)."

**The fast power trap.** `half = power(x, n / 2)` once, then `half * half`, is O(log n). Writing `power(x, n / 2) * power(x, n / 2)` makes two calls per level: 1 + 2 + 4 + ... + n, about 2n calls, so **O(n)**. Depth alone doesn't give the runtime; the number of calls per level does.

**Memoization.** Naive Fibonacci recomputes the same small values over and over. Cache each answer the first time, and each value from 0 to n is computed once: **O(n)**. That's top-down dynamic programming.

**Space is depth, not calls.** Only one path of frames is on the stack at a time. Naive Fibonacci makes O(2ⁿ) calls but uses only **O(n)** stack space. Fast power uses O(log n).

questions.question: True or false: naive Fibonacci uses O(2ⁿ) stack space, because it makes O(2ⁿ) calls.
True or false: memoized Fibonacci runs in O(n) because each value from 0 to n is computed only once.

# Write It: Fast Power

Midterm problem 17: compute xⁿ in **O(log n)** by halving n instead of subtracting 1.

| n is… | then |
|---|---|
| 0 | x⁰ = 1 (base case) |
| even | xⁿ = xⁿᐟ² · xⁿᐟ² |
| odd | xⁿ = x · xⁿᐟ² · xⁿᐟ² |

Integer division makes the odd case work: 13 / 2 is 6, and x¹³ = x · x⁶ · x⁶.

```
power(x, 13) -> power(x, 6) -> power(x, 3) -> power(x, 1) -> power(x, 0)
```

# Write It: allPositive and isSorted

Two more checks for the sensor array, both "is every element OK?" questions.

**allPositive** was on Quiz 5. This time recursion shrinks the **length** instead of moving an index: look at the last element, then ask the same question about the first `length - 1`.

```cpp
bool allPositive(const int arr[], int length) {
    if (length == 0) return true;      // base case, and handles an empty array
    return arr[length - 1] > 0 && allPositive(arr, length - 1);
}
```

Why is an empty array `true`? Because there's no element that breaks the rule. It's also exactly the base case the recursion needs. An equivalent way to write the second line: `if (arr[length - 1] <= 0) return false; return allPositive(arr, length - 1);`

> [!warning]
> The Quiz 5 rubric took points off for each of these:
> - no `length == 0` base case, or one that returns `false` (an empty array is `true`)
> - testing `< 0` instead of `<= 0`: 0 is not positive
> - reading `arr[length]` (one past the end) instead of `arr[length - 1]`, or always checking `arr[0]`
> - a recursive call that doesn't shrink `length`, or whose result is ignored instead of returned
> - a path that never returns `false`, or that falls off the end without returning
> - any loop: the question says no loops

```

{1, 3, 2, 4}: 1 ≤ 3, 3 > 2           -> false (stops right there)
```

# Write It: isSub with an Index Helper

The robot logs every move it makes. A demo script lists the moves that **must** happen, in order. Did the log include them all, in that order, possibly with other moves in between? That was the midterm bonus: is `s` a **subsequence** of `t`?

"ace" is a subsequence of "abcde" (a, then c, then e). "aec" isn't: the letters are there, but not in that order.

The professor's first version shrinks both strings with `substr`:

```cpp
bool isSub(const std::string& s, const std::string& t) {
    if (s.size() == 0) return true;     // matched every letter of s
    if (t.size() == 0) return false;    // ran out of t first
    if (s[0] == t[0]) return isSub(s.substr(1), t.substr(1));
    else return isSub(s, t.substr(1));
}
```

If the first letters match, use up one letter of each. If not, skip a letter of `t` and keep looking.

**The order of the base cases matters.** Swap them and `isSub("", "")` returns false, and so does any match that finishes on the very last letter of `t`.

The second version uses **indices** instead of copying strings, with a helper, the same pattern as the palindrome:

| s index | t index | compare | action |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | 0 | a, a | match: both move |
| 1 | 1 | c, b | skip t |
| 1 | 2 | c, c | match: both move |
| 2 | 3 | e, d | skip t |
| 2 | 4 | e, e | match: both move |
| 3 | 5 | | s used up: **true** |

## Assignment

1. [ ] Complete `isSubHelper(s, t, sIndex, tIndex)` recursively: is `s` from `sIndex` on a subsequence of `t` from `tIndex` on? Base cases in this order: `s` used up → `true`, then `t` used up → `false`. The helper must call **itself**.
2. [ ] Complete `isSub(s, t)` by calling `isSubHelper(s, t, 0, 0)`. Don't use `substr`.

# Push, Pop, Enqueue, Dequeue

A **stack** is LIFO: last in, first out. You only touch the top. A **queue** is FIFO: first in, first out. Things join at the back and leave from the front.

![three edits pushed, then undo pops the newest](courses/diagrams/af081924-b832-5177-a1de-99b2919b6f03/lifo.svg)

![jobs joining at the back and leaving at the front](courses/diagrams/44a628da-add2-5243-bf84-7060ba8e69b8/steps.svg)

| Stack | Queue |
|---|---|
| `push(e)`: put e on top | `enqueue(e)`: add e at the back |
| `pop()`: remove and return the top | `dequeue()`: remove and return the front |
| `top()`: look, don't remove | `front()`: look, don't remove |

`pop`, `top`, `dequeue` and `front` on an empty one throw an exception in the lecture's ADT.

**How to trace on paper.** Write the contents in one row, always in the same direction (bottom to top for a stack, front to back for a queue). Cross out what leaves. `top()` and `front()` change nothing; skip them.

Browser history is a stack: each visit pushes, Back pops. Push A, B, C; go back twice (pop C, pop B); visit D (push D). The stack is now `A D`, and you're on D.

Undo, the back button and the call stack are stacks. Printers, waiting lines and keyboard buffers are queues. A stack **reverses** order; a queue **keeps** it.

Starting with an empty queue: enqueue(5), enqueue(3), dequeue(), enqueue(8), enqueue(1), front(), dequeue(), enqueue(6). Front to back, the queue is:

lessons.readme:
# Postfix: Convert and Evaluate

In **postfix** the operator comes after its operands: `A + B` is `A B +`. It needs no parentheses and no precedence rules, which is why compilers convert to it.

| Infix | Postfix |
|---|---|
| A * B + C | A B * C + |
| A * (B + C) | A B C + * |
| A + B * C | A B C * + |
| A - B - C | A B - C - |

The operands never change order. Only the operators move.

**Convert by hand:** parenthesize every operation, move each operator just past its closing `)`, drop the parentheses. Equal precedence groups from the left.

```
A * B + C  ->  ((A * B) + C)  ->  ((A B) * C) +  ->  A B * C +
```

**Convert with a stack** (the version he traces):

1. Operand: output it.
2. `(`: push it.
3. Operator: pop and output operators of **equal or higher** precedence (stop at a `(`), then push this one.
4. `)`: pop and output until the `(`, and discard the `(`. At the end, pop everything.

![the operator stack at eight points of the conversion](courses/diagrams/2600d66e-d1ec-5196-a964-2a7ae57b6fdc/steps.svg)

**Evaluate with a stack:** a number is pushed; an operator pops **b**, then pops **a**, and pushes `a op b`.

![the stack while evaluating a postfix expression, six steps](courses/diagrams/647f771d-d11c-50c8-b98a-d09f22874b27/steps.svg)

> [!warning]
> The **first** pop is the **right** operand. It doesn't matter for `+` and `*`, but `8 2 -` is 6, not -6.

# The Circular Array Queue

A queue in a plain array either shifts on every dequeue (O(n)) or creeps off the end. The fix is to treat the array as a **circle**: after slot N − 1 comes slot 0.

- `f` is the index of the front element
- `r` is one **past** the last element, and that slot is always empty

```cpp
// enqueue
Q[r] = e;
r = (r + 1) % N;

// dequeue
e = Q[f];
f = (f + 1) % N;
```

| | Formula |
|---|---|
| empty | `f == r` |
| size | `(N - f + r) % N` |
| full | `size() == N - 1` |

![a circular queue, normal and wrapped around](courses/diagrams/247a40ca-60e7-5b5a-8c06-512e8bd32e66/rings.svg)

**Why N − 1?** If all N slots could fill, `r` would wrap onto `f`, and full would look exactly like empty. Wasting one slot keeps `f == r` meaning only "empty". So **an array of N slots holds N − 1 elements**.

Adding N before `%` in the size formula keeps the wrapped case from going negative: N = 8, f = 6, r = 2 gives (8 − 6 + 2) % 8 = 4.

**Tracing.** Draw the N boxes and keep `f` and `r` in two columns. Each enqueue moves only `r`, each dequeue moves only `f`. Queue order starts at `f`, not at slot 0.

![f and r wrapping past the end of an eight-slot array](courses/diagrams/6d778345-a364-54ad-a4cd-00c0d70cc28d/steps.svg)

lessons.readme:
# Stack, Queue and Deque Costs

Stacks and queues only touch their ends, so almost everything is O(1). The questions are about the few exceptions.

**Array stack push.** With a fixed array, push writes one slot: O(1), and it throws when full. With a growable array, a push into a full one copies everything first: **O(n) worst case**. Averaged over n pushes (the amortized cost):

| Growth strategy | n pushes | Amortized per push |
|---|---|---|
| add a constant c slots | O(n²) | O(n) |
| **double** the size | O(n) | **O(1)** |

Pop, top, size and isEmpty are O(1) on both array and linked stacks. Linked stacks are easier to write; array stacks are faster and use less memory (no pointer per element).

**Queue on a singly linked list.** With `head` and `tail`, put the **front at head** and the back at tail. Then enqueue is insertBack (O(1) with tail) and dequeue is removeFront (O(1)). Flip them and dequeue becomes removeBack, which is O(n) on a singly linked list.

**Deque** (double-ended queue): insert and remove at both ends.

| | Circular array, doubling | Singly (head + tail) | Doubly |
|---|---|---|---|
| insertFront / insertBack | O(1) amortized | O(1) | O(1) |
| removeFront | O(1) | O(1) | O(1) |
| removeBack | O(1) | **O(n)** | O(1) |

> [!warning]
> "Amortized O(1)" and "O(1) worst case" are different claims. A T/F that says doubling push is O(1) "even in the worst case" is false.

lessons.readme:
# Three Searches, Three Costs

A lookup costs the number of **key comparisons** it makes, and n is the number of records. There are three ways to look, and each one has a trap he likes to set.

**Sequential search** checks `arr[0]`, `arr[1]`, … until it hits the key or runs out. Best case is the key at the front: 1 comparison. Worst case is the key in the last slot **or not there at all**: n comparisons, O(n).

![sequential search checks cells from the left](courses/diagrams/64173228-1f0b-5351-8b96-596d4e145ee5/scan.svg)

- **Sorting the list doesn't fix the worst case.** On `104 117 131 152 166`, a search for 140 can quit at 152. But a search for 170, or for 166, still walks the whole list. Worst case stays **O(n)**.
- **Put the popular keys first.** The key at position k costs k comparisons. If a few keys get most of the lookups, move them to the front once. Sorting by name doesn't help at all; only what sits near the front matters.

**Binary search** looks at the middle of a **sorted** array. If the middle key is smaller than the key you want, the key can only be on the right; if bigger, only on the left. One look throws away half, so it takes about log₂ n looks: **O(log n)**. A million records need about 20.

```
first = 0, last = n - 1
while first <= last
    mid = first + (last - first) / 2
    if arr[mid] == key      return mid
    else if arr[mid] < key  first = mid + 1
    else                    last = mid - 1
return -1
```

Trace a search for 31 in `3 8 12 19 24 31 40` (indexes 0 to 6): mid = 3 holds 19 < 31, so first = 4. Then mid = 4 + (6 − 4)/2 = 5 holds 31. Found after looking at indexes 3 and 5.

It needs **random access**, jumping to `arr[mid]` in O(1). On a linked list, just reaching the middle is O(n), so binary search there isn't O(log n).

**Insert or delete in a sorted array** is the trap. Binary search finds the spot in O(log n), but then every key after it has to shift one slot to open or close the gap. The shift is O(n), so the whole operation is **O(n)**.

> [!warning]
> "Binary search is O(log n), so deleting from a sorted array is O(log n)" is the false "because" he writes. Finding is fast; shifting is not.

lessons.readme:
# Write It: Iterative Binary Search

At the start of each semester the registrar sorts the directory by ID. Now we can do much better than checking every entry.

Look at the middle entry. If it's the key, we're done. If it's **smaller** than the key, the key can only be in the right half; if it's bigger, only the left half. Either way, one look throws away half of what's left. That's **binary search**.

It's how you look up a word in a big paper dictionary. You don't start at page 1: you open it near the middle, check the word at the top of the page, and ignore the half that can't hold your word. Then you do the same to the half that's left.

![a large dictionary lying open near its middle](courses/diagrams/944c136f-87d3-554c-b4c7-302c85fe99f1/dictionary.jpg)
*Image: Cullen328, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons.*

We keep two indexes, `first` and `last`, around the part that's still possible, and compute `mid = first + (last - first) / 2`. Here's a search for 189:

![binary search for 189, steps 1 and 2](courses/diagrams/944c136f-87d3-554c-b4c7-302c85fe99f1/steps_a.svg)

![binary search for 189, steps 3 and 4](courses/diagrams/944c136f-87d3-554c-b4c7-302c85fe99f1/steps_b.svg)

In the pictures f, m and l are short for `first`, `mid` and `last`, and red cells have been ruled out. If `first` ever passes `last`, nothing is left, and the key isn't there.

**Why `first + (last - first) / 2`?** It's the same as `(first + last) / 2` on paper, but `first + last` can overflow an `int` on a huge array. Integer division rounds down.

> [!warning]
> Binary search needs a **sorted** array with **random access** (jumping to `arr[mid]` in O(1)). On an unsorted array it gives wrong answers, and on a linked list just reaching the middle takes O(n).

## Assignment

Add binary search to `search.h`. It must be O(log n): the tests time it on a million IDs.

1. [ ] Set `first = 0` and `last = n - 1`.
2. [ ] While `first <= last`: compute `mid`. If `arr[mid] == key`, return `mid`. Else if `arr[mid] < key`, set `first = mid + 1`. Else set `last = mid - 1`.
3. [ ] After the loop, return `-1`.

lessons.readme:
# Hashing Rules He Tests

A **hash table** skips comparing keys altogether. It has m **buckets**, and a **hash function** turns each key into a bucket number, its **home bucket**. A lookup computes the hash and looks only there.

![buckets by first letter](courses/diagrams/ef9f7418-bc35-5c8b-9869-01af0598cc33/letters.svg)

Look at bucket C: "CHEM" and "CMPE" landed together. Two keys in one bucket are a **collision**. With a good hash and a table that isn't too full, buckets stay short, so insert and lookup are **O(1) on average**. In the **worst case** every key lands in one bucket, and you're back to **O(n)**. Any T/F that says "always O(1)" or "O(1) even in the worst case" is false.

**What makes a hash function good:**

- **Deterministic.** The same key gives the same bucket every time. Otherwise you'd store a key in one bucket and look for it in another. This one is required, not just nice.
- **Uses the whole key.** `h(s) = s[0] % m` only reads the first character, so "plum" and "plump" get the same number and collide for **every** m. Keys with different first letters might collide for some m, but they aren't forced to.
- **Uniform and fast.** Spread keys evenly, and be cheap to compute. Being hard to reverse is **not** a goal; that's for cryptographic hashes.

**Load factor** α = n / m, records over buckets. 1,500 records in 2,000 buckets is α = 0.75. Low α wastes memory; high α means more collisions. Grow the table as α approaches 1.

There are two ways to handle collisions, and the capacity rule differs:

| | Where colliding keys go | Can α exceed 1? |
|---|---|---|
| **Separate chaining** | a linked list per bucket | yes: 2,000 records in 1,000 buckets is α = 2, just slower |
| **Open addressing** (linear probing) | another bucket in the same array | no: one record per bucket, so at most m records |

lessons.readme:
# Deletes, Chaining and Clustering

**Deleting breaks probe paths.** Say 23, 43 and 13 all hashed to 3 and sit in buckets 3, 4, 5. Delete 23 by marking bucket 3 `EMPTY`. Now `find(43)` starts at 3, sees empty, and says "not found", though 43 is right there in bucket 4.

![bucket 3 emptied; find for 43 stops there and never reaches bucket 4](courses/diagrams/6ff6d64c-8fd1-5e87-b102-7cfa491ebc7c/broken.svg)

The fix the class uses is a **tombstone**: mark the bucket `DELETED`. It means "a record used to be here, keep looking." Find probes past it; insert may reuse it. Delete stays O(1).

![a tombstone keeps the chain intact](courses/diagrams/6ff6d64c-8fd1-5e87-b102-7cfa491ebc7c/tomb.svg)

So "a search can stop at an empty bucket" is only true if nothing was ever deleted, or if deletes leave tombstones.

**Primary clustering.** In linear probing, full buckets form runs, and a run grows: any key whose home lands **anywhere** in it walks to its end and joins it. That's why linear probing is fast when the table is mostly empty and falls off sharply as it fills. A miss has to walk to the end of the cluster, while a hit stops partway, so **misses get worse much faster**:

| α | Successful probes | Unsuccessful probes |
|---|---|---|
| 0.5 | 1.5 | 2.5 |
| 0.75 | 2.5 | 8.5 |
| 0.99 | 50.5 | about 5000 |

Worst case, one giant cluster, is **O(n)** for find and for insert.

**Separate chaining** has no clustering. Colliding keys go into that bucket's own linked list, so they never spill into neighbors. Deleting is just unlinking a node, and α can go above 1. A lookup costs the length of one chain: α on average, n if every key lands in the same bucket.

A linear probing table deletes by setting the bucket to EMPTY. Now some finds report "not found" for keys that are in the table. Which change fixes this most directly?
answers: Double the table size after every delete
Mark deleted buckets DELETED and probe past them
Make find stop at DELETED buckets as well
questions.answer: Mark deleted buckets DELETED and probe past them

questions.question: Separate chaining suffers from primary clustering, because colliding keys are stored in neighboring buckets.
A linear probing table fills up, so α goes from 0.5 toward 1. What happens?
answers: Hits and misses slow down equally
Misses slow down much faster than hits
Only inserts slow down; finds stay O(1)
Nothing: every key has a home bucket
questions.answer: Misses slow down much faster than hits

# Write It: Linear Probing Insert

Lab 7's table keeps a **state** in each bucket, `EMPTY`, `OCCUPIED` or `DELETED`, so any int can be a real key. `HashTable` is a struct of three parallel vectors (`keys`, `values`, `state`), and `capacity()` is m. The home bucket of key k is `k % m`.

- If k is **already** in the table, replace its value and return `true`.
- Otherwise store it in the first `EMPTY` bucket on its probe path and return `true`.
- Return `false` only if there's no room.

Check for the key first, then look for space. A full table can still update a key it already holds.

**On paper** the same idea is the keys-only version from the last lessons: `idx = (home + i) % m;` to step, `table[idx] = key;` to store. Here it's the same loop with a state check.

lessons.readme:
# Bubble, Selection, Insertion: Tell Them Apart

All three are O(n²) on a Big O sheet, so he tests what makes them different: what one pass does, and which inputs help.

**Bubble sort.** Each pass walks left to right and swaps neighbors that are out of order, so the largest remaining key gets carried to the end. After pass i (from 0), the last i + 1 keys are the largest, sorted and **final**. If a whole pass makes **no swaps**, every neighbor pair is in order, so the array is sorted. (The lecture's version keeps going anyway, so its best case is still O(n²) comparisons.)

**Selection sort.** Pass i scans everything that's left, finds the minimum, and swaps it into position i. After pass i the first i + 1 keys are the smallest, sorted and **final**. The scan can't know the minimum is already in front until it has looked at everything, so it makes n(n − 1)/2 comparisons on **every** input, sorted included. It does only one swap per pass: O(n) swaps. Long swaps can jump a key past an equal one, so it's **not stable**. And it can't place even its first key until all the data is there.

**Insertion sort.** Like sorting a hand of cards: the left part is sorted, and each pass slides the next key left into its place. After pass i (from 1), the first i + 1 keys are sorted **among themselves** but not final: a small key later can push them all right. On sorted input every pass stops after one comparison, so its best case is **O(n)**. Because each new key just slides into what's already sorted, it can sort data that arrives **a piece at a time** (online).

One pass of each on `5 2 8 1 4`:

| Sort | After the first pass | What happened |
|---|---|---|
| Bubble | `2 5 1 4 8` | 8 was carried to the end |
| Selection | `1 2 8 5 4` | min 1 swapped with index 0 |
| Insertion (i = 1) | `2 5 8 1 4` | 2 slid left past 5 |

| | Comparisons | Best case | Stable |
|---|---|---|---|
| Bubble | always n(n − 1)/2 | O(n²) (lecture version) | yes |
| Selection | always n(n − 1)/2 | O(n²) | **no** |
| Insertion | n − 1 sorted, n(n − 1)/2 reverse | **O(n)** | yes |

All three are in place: O(1) extra space.

# Write It: One Insertion Pass

Selection sort compares O(n²) times even on a leaderboard that's already in order. Can we do better when the data is nearly sorted?

**Insertion sort** is how you sort a hand of cards. The left part is sorted; each pass takes the next key and **inserts** it where it belongs among the keys to its left.

![a fanned-out hand of playing cards, not yet in order](courses/diagrams/3aff566f-934b-5d8d-b940-2289e4fb61d5/hand-of-cards.jpg)
*Image: Jiahui Huang, CC BY-SA 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons.*

Pick up the cards one at a time. Each new card slides left past the bigger cards already in your hand until it reaches its spot, and the cards to its left are always in order.

The professor's version doesn't swap. It saves the new key in `temp`, shifts every bigger key one spot right to open a hole, and drops `temp` into the hole:

```
temp = A[i]
j = i-1
if temp < A[j]
    while j >= 0 and temp < A[j]
        A[j+1] = A[j]
        j--
    A[j+1] = temp
```

Here's pass i = 2 on the lecture's example, where `temp = 3`:

![insertion sort shifting keys to make a hole for 3](courses/diagrams/3aff566f-934b-5d8d-b940-2289e4fb61d5/hole.svg)

Each step is one copy into the hole, and `temp` is written once at the end.

Two details matter. The `j >= 0` test comes **first**, so when `temp` belongs at the very front we stop before reading `A[-1]`. And the `if` guard means a key that's already in place costs one comparison and **no writes** at all.

## Assignment

1. [ ] Complete `insertionPass(A, i)`: insert `A[i]` into the sorted keys `A[0..i-1]` using `temp`, the shifting and the hole, exactly as above. You can assume `i >= 1`.

# Write It: Merge Two Sorted Arrays

O(n²) is fine for a few hundred scores. On a whole semester of games it isn't. To do better we need a new idea, and it starts small.

The arcade has two cabinets, and each one keeps its own leaderboard already sorted. To build one combined board, we don't need to sort from scratch. We can **merge**:

1. Look at the front of each list.
2. Take the smaller one and append it to the output.
3. When one list runs out, copy the rest of the other. That costs **no** comparisons.

```
merge(A, B):
    S = empty
    while A and B are not empty
        if A.first() <= B.first()
            S.insertLast(A.removeFirst())
        else
            S.insertLast(B.removeFirst())
    copy the rest of A, then the rest of B, into S
```

Here's `merge([2, 5, 8], [3, 6, 9, 13])`. Blue is each list's front, red is already used, amber is what was just taken:

![merge steps 1 and 2](courses/diagrams/6355c68e-d711-5b6e-87a6-f6a013a94020/m1.svg)

![merge steps 3 and 4](courses/diagrams/6355c68e-d711-5b6e-87a6-f6a013a94020/m2.svg)

![merge step 5 and the leftovers](courses/diagrams/6355c68e-d711-5b6e-87a6-f6a013a94020/m3.svg)

Five comparisons, then 9 and 13 are copied over for free.

**On paper** (Quiz 7), merge works on plain arrays with three indexes: `i` into A, `j` into B, `k` into the output S. The skeleton is given and you fill in the two branches:

```cpp
while (i < lenA && j < lenB) {
    if (A[i] <= B[j]) {
        S[k] = A[i];   // copy A's front into S
        i++;           // and move past it in A
    }
    else {
        S[k] = B[j];
        j++;
    }
    k++;               // already in the skeleton, after the if/else
}
while (i < lenA) S[k++] = A[i++];
while (j < lenB) S[k++] = B[j++];
```

> [!warning]
> - Write into **S**. Nothing gets swapped or written back into A or B; there's no `temp`.
> - Each branch advances only the index it read from: `i++` with A, `j++` with B. Forgetting it copies the same key forever.
> - Don't add your own `k++` inside a branch when the skeleton already has one after the if/else, or every other slot of S is skipped.

Why `<=` and not `<`? On a tie it takes from A first, and A's keys came first originally. That's what will make merge sort **stable**.

You've seen this before: it's the linked list merge from the Linked Lists chapter, but on vectors.

## Assignment

1. [ ] `merge(a, b)`: both are sorted ascending. Return a new sorted vector with every key from both. Use `<=` so ties take from `a` first.

# Partition: The Pivot Lands Home

Quicksort picks a **pivot** and partitions the array around it: every key left of the pivot is ≤ it, every key right of it is ≥ it. Then the pivot is in its **final** sorted position, and nobody ever moves it again. The two sides are **not** sorted yet; recursion handles them.

**Checking an answer choice** ("which array could follow partitioning around 5?"): find the pivot in the option, then check that everything to its left is ≤ it and everything to its right is ≥ it. Order inside each side doesn't matter. One key on the wrong side rules the option out.

`3 1 4 2 5 9 7 8` passes for pivot 5. `3 1 7 2 5 9 4 8` fails: 7 sits left of 5.

**Lomuto partition**, the class scheme, uses the last key as the pivot. `i` marks where the next key ≤ pivot goes:

```
Partition(S, lo, hi)
    pivot = S[hi]
    i = lo
    for j = lo to hi-1
        if S[j] <= pivot
            swap S[i] with S[j]
            i++
    swap S[i] with S[hi]
    return i
```

Here's the lecture's trace on `7 3 8 0 9 2 1 6`:

![Lomuto partition traced step by step](courses/diagrams/c3b154bb-e743-5f7d-9c7a-33d2703a968a/trace.svg)

A quick check before you trace: the return value is lo plus the number of other keys ≤ the pivot. Here 3, 0, 2 and 1 are ≤ 6, so 6 lands at index 4. Partition scans once, so it's **O(n)**.

Lomuto partition (pivot = last key) runs on `5 8 2 9 1 4`. What is the array afterward?
After one partition, the keys to the left of the pivot are in sorted order.
After a partition, the pivot is in the position it will have in the fully sorted array.

lessons.readme:
# Write It: Lomuto Partition

There are many ways to partition. The class uses the **Lomuto** scheme: the pivot is the **last** key, and one scan from `lo` to `hi - 1` builds `[keys ≤ pivot] [pivot] [keys > pivot]`.

The index `i` marks where the next key ≤ pivot will go. Everything before `i` is already known to be ≤ pivot. When `j` finds another small key, swap it to `i` and move `i` up:

```
Partition(S, lo, hi)
    pivot = S[hi]
    i = lo
    for j = lo to hi-1
        if S[j] <= pivot
            swap S[i] with S[j]
            i++
    swap S[i] with S[hi]
    return i
```

Here's the lecture's trace on `7 3 8 0 9 2 1 6`:

![Lomuto partition traced step by step](courses/diagrams/c3b154bb-e743-5f7d-9c7a-33d2703a968a/trace.svg)

When the loop ends, `S[lo..i-1]` is L, and `S[i..hi-1]` is G. The last swap trades the pivot with the first key of G, which drops the pivot right between them.

It scans the array once, so partition is **O(n)**: exactly hi − lo comparisons.

## Assignment

1. [ ] `partition(S, lo, hi)`: Lomuto, exactly as above, pivot = `S[hi]`. Return the pivot's final index. Only touch `S[lo..hi]`.

The tests check the whole array afterward, so follow the steps exactly; another partition scheme would leave the keys in a different order.

lessons.readme:
# Quicksort's Worst Case and the Sort Table

Quicksort's speed depends on where the pivot lands. If L gets k keys, G gets the rest:

T(n) = T(k) + T(n − k − 1) + O(n)

**Balanced splits.** The pivot lands near the middle, the recursion is about log₂ n levels deep, and each level partitions about n keys: **O(n log n)**. Even lopsided splits like 25/75 keep it O(log n) deep, so the average case is O(n log n).

**Sorted input with the last key as pivot.** The pivot is always the largest key, everything goes to L, G is empty. The recursion is a chain n levels deep:

![quicksort on sorted input makes a chain](courses/diagrams/750f48ce-8151-52fe-ad47-e9ef69e427a8/chain.svg)

(n − 1) + (n − 2) + … + 1 = n(n − 1)/2 comparisons = **O(n²)**. Reverse-sorted input and all-equal keys do the same. A first-key pivot on sorted input fails the same way. So "quicksort is O(n log n)" is only true when the splits are balanced.

The whole table:

| Sort | Best | Average | Worst | Extra space | Stable |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Bubble | O(n²) | O(n²) | O(n²) | O(1) | yes |
| Selection | O(n²) | O(n²) | O(n²) | O(1) | **no** |
| Insertion | **O(n)** | O(n²) | O(n²) | O(1) | yes |
| Merge | O(n log n) | O(n log n) | O(n log n) | **O(n)** | yes |
| Quick | O(n log n) | O(n log n) | **O(n²)** | O(log n) stack | **no** |
| Heap | O(n log n) | O(n log n) | O(n log n) | O(log n) stack | **no** |

**In place** means it rearranges inside the array: every sort here except merge sort. **Stable** means equal keys keep their original order: bubble, insertion and merge. Selection, quick and heap sort swap keys long distances, past equal keys.

Picking one: stable or a guaranteed O(n log n) worst case means merge sort. Fastest in practice on an array in memory, when stability doesn't matter, means quicksort.

# Practice Like the Exam: Sorting (True/False)

The professor's quizzes open with five True/False sentences. On sorting, the traps come from a small set of shapes:

- **Swapped pair.** "Sort A does X, while sort B does Y" with the properties traded between the two sorts. Check each half against the comparison table, one sort at a time.
- **Wrong "because".** "Sort A is fast on this input because of some plausible reason." The conclusion may even be true. Ask whether that reason is what the code actually does.
- **Average dressed up as worst.** "Quicksort is O(n log n), so it never takes longer than that." Look for the input that breaks it: with the last key as pivot, sorted input.
- **Which version?** His bubble sort has no early exit, and his insertion sort has the `if (temp < A[j])` guard. Best cases and counts depend on the exact loop.
- **Invariant stated plainly.** "After pass i, the first i + 1 keys are…" These are often True, but check which end of the array and whether the keys are **final**.

About two of the five are True.

True or false: "After pass i of selection sort (counting passes from i = 0), the first i + 1 keys of the array are the i + 1 smallest keys, each in its final position."

lessons.readme:
# Traversals Without Tears

The three recursive traversals differ only in **when** you visit the root compared to its subtrees. Left always goes before right.

| Order | Steps | Tell |
|---|---|---|
| **Pre-order** | root, left, right | starts with the root |
| **In-order** | left, root, right | root is somewhere in the middle |
| **Post-order** | left, right, root | ends with the root |

**The one-walk trick.** All three make the same trip around the tree, counterclockwise from the root, touching each node three times. Pre-order records a node when you pass it on its **left**, in-order when you pass **underneath**, post-order when you pass on its **right**:

![a dashed path circling the tree counterclockwise from the root, with a dot on the left, bottom and right of each node](courses/diagrams/b0d45bda-aa29-5099-b50a-0e1377ea7eef/walk.svg)

Amber dots read 1 2 4 5 3 6 (pre), blue 4 2 5 1 3 6 (in), green 4 5 2 6 3 1 (post). Finish a whole subtree before moving on: after 2 in pre-order come 4 and 5, not 3.

Facts he turns into T/F:

- **In-order of a BST is sorted**, because everything left is smaller and everything right is larger. For a plain binary tree it means nothing.
- **Post-order is the order to free every node.** Children go before the parent, so you never read `left` or `right` out of a node you already deleted.
- **No left children means pre-order equals in-order.** With an empty left subtree, "left, root, right" and "root, left, right" both visit the root first.

**Expression trees.** Operators are internal nodes, numbers are leaves, and the shape replaces parentheses. Pre-order gives prefix, in-order gives infix (with the parentheses lost), post-order gives postfix:

![the expression tree for 2 * (3 + 4 - (5 - 6))](courses/diagrams/e46120d2-7159-5bce-97c7-fddf834656fd/expr.svg)

| Traversal | Result |
|---|---|
| Pre-order | `* 2 - + 3 4 - 5 6` |
| In-order | `2 * 3 + 4 - 5 - 6` |
| Post-order | `2 3 4 + 5 6 - - *` |

# Write It: countNodes and countLeaves

Spartan Maps wants a stats line: how many buildings are in the tree, and how many sit at the bottom as leaves.

Almost every binary tree function has the same recipe:

1. **Base case:** handle the empty tree (`nullptr`).
2. **Recursive case:** ask the left and right subtrees the same question, then combine their answers with this node.

Here it is for a function we won't need, the sum of all keys:

```cpp
int sumTree(TreeNode* t) {
    if (t == nullptr) return 0;                       // empty: nothing to add
    return t->info + sumTree(t->left) + sumTree(t->right);
}
```

Counting nodes is the same shape, adding 1 per node instead of `info`.

Counting leaves needs one more case. A node is a leaf only when **both** children are `nullptr`. A node with one child is internal, so it isn't counted; its child might be.

![a tree with its leaves marked](courses/diagrams/bcd240ef-eaa4-502f-80c1-4f347dd40041/leaves.svg)

Lab 8's `BinaryTree` also has `isEmpty()`, which is just `root == nullptr`.

## Assignment

1. [ ] `countNodes(t)`: the number of nodes in the tree. An empty tree has 0.
2. [ ] `countLeaves(t)`: the number of nodes with no children. An empty tree has 0.

# Write It: Recursive Tree Height

Height will decide how fast every BST operation is, so let's compute it.

The recipe is the same as last lesson. The height of a tree is one more than the height of its **taller** subtree, because the deepest node lives down one of the two sides:

```
height(t) = 1 + max(height(left), height(right))
```

What about the base case? A single node has height 0, and its two subtrees are empty. For the formula to give 1 + max(?, ?) = 0, an empty tree must have height **−1**. That's why the lecture and Lab 8 define it that way.

![subtree heights](courses/diagrams/9562a2fc-cb78-5307-9a28-233a647fb510/heights.svg)

Notice that the deepest path here goes **right**. A function that only follows the left side, or that picks a side by which child exists, gets this tree wrong. Always ask both sides.

> [!warning]
> Don't return 0 for an empty tree. Then a single node would have height 1, and every answer would be one too big.

## Assignment

1. [ ] Complete `height(t)`: the largest depth of any node. An empty tree is −1, and a single node is 0.

# Is It Really a BST?

In a **binary search tree**, each node's key is **larger than every key in its left subtree** and **smaller than every key in its right subtree**. The rule is about whole subtrees, not just children.

![a BST next to a tree that breaks the rule](courses/diagrams/77551e4c-8794-5422-b075-2e68e786b588/rule.svg)

In the right-hand tree, 55 is fine next to its parent 30. But it's in 50's **left** subtree, and 55 > 50. So that tree is not a BST, even though every parent-child pair looks right. That's his favorite T/F: "a tree is a BST if each node's left child is smaller and right child is larger" is **false**.

**How to check by hand.** Carry a range down the tree. The root can be anything. Going left from key k, everything below must be < k; going right, > k. Every node has to fit between the limits set by **all** its ancestors:

![allowed ranges carried down the tree](courses/diagrams/69d0d159-2e35-56dd-ab68-08ec9242656a/ranges.svg)

55 must be between 30 and 50. It isn't. Caught.

**Faster check: in-order.** In-order of a BST is sorted. List the in-order traversal; if any key is smaller than the one before it, it's not a BST.

Worked example. In this tree, 15 sits in 20's left subtree and 10's right subtree, so its allowed range is (10, 20):

```
        20
      /    \
    10      30
   /  \    /  \
  5   15  25   40
```

Replace 15 with 12 or 18 and it's still a BST. Replace it with 22 and it isn't: 22 > 10 is fine for its parent, but 22 > 20 breaks the root's rule.

```
   /  \    /  \
  5   15  25   40
```

It is a BST if each child pair is in order
It is not a BST: 11 comes after 12
