lessons.title: Height Decides Everything
lessons.readme:
# Height Decides Everything

BST search follows **one path** from the root down, one comparison per level. Insert does the same walk and adds a leaf where it falls off. Delete walks down too. So all three are **O(h)**, where h is the height.

What h is depends on the shape, and the shape depends on the **insert order**:

![sorted inserts make a chain; shuffled inserts make a bushy tree](courses/diagrams/f9d31fac-8b6c-56c0-a1dd-76d909d2b484/orders.svg)

- **Sorted input:** every new key is the largest so far, so it always goes right. The tree is a chain with h = n − 1, and search is **O(n)**. Reverse-sorted input does the same on the left.
- **Shuffled input:** early keys land near the middle and split the rest, so h stays close to log₂ n.

So the worst-case BST search is **O(n)**, not O(log n). "Each comparison throws away a subtree, so it's O(log n)" is the false "because": in a chain, the subtree you throw away is empty.

**Shortest tree from a given set of keys:** insert the **median first**, then the medians of each half, and so on. For 1 to 7: `4 2 6 1 3 5 7` gives height 2. Lab 8 shuffles its input for the same reason.

**Counting nodes.** Level k holds at most 2ᵏ nodes. A **perfect** tree of height k fills every level: 1 + 2 + 4 + … + 2ᵏ = **2ᵏ⁺¹ − 1** nodes. Height 3 gives 15 nodes. Turned around, n nodes fit in a height of about log₂ n at best and n − 1 at worst.

| Shape | Height | Search, insert, delete |
|---|---|---|
| balanced | about log₂ n | O(log n) |
| chain | n − 1 | O(n) |

# Write It: BST Insert

New buildings open, and Spartan Maps needs to add them. Where does a new key go?

Search for it. If it's not there, the search walks off the tree at exactly the spot where it **would** have been. Put it there. So **new nodes are always added as leaves**, and nothing else in the tree moves.

Here's `insert(50)` on the lecture's tree:

![insert 50 becomes the left child of 65](courses/diagrams/e22d1689-978f-50b1-9ed0-4f5d17b1a7ad/insert50.svg)

The lecture's insert is a loop, like search, with one special case for an empty tree:

```
insert(key):
    if root == nullptr:  root = new node(key); return
    cur = root
    while true
        if key < cur->info
            if cur->left == nullptr:  cur->left = new node(key); return
            cur = cur->left
        else if key > cur->info
            (the same on the right)
        else
            return            // duplicate key: do nothing
```

Since search is O(h) and adding the leaf is O(1), insert is **O(h)** too.

> [!note]
> Lab 8's BST is a template that must work for any `T` with only `<` and `==`. So don't write `key > cur->info`. Write `cur->info < key`, which means the same thing.

## Assignment

1. [ ] Complete `insert(root, key)`. Add `key` as a new leaf where the BST rule puts it. If the tree is empty, `root` becomes the new node (that's why it's passed by reference). If `key` is already in the tree, do nothing.

lessons.readme:
# BST Delete: Three Cases by Hand

Delete depends on how many children the node has. The tree must still follow the BST rule afterward.

**Case 1: a leaf.** Set the **parent's** pointer to `nullptr`, then free the node. Here `delete(34)`, where 34 is 39's left child, is `39->left = nullptr; free 34`. Freeing it without fixing 39 leaves 39 pointing at freed memory.

![removing leaf 34](courses/diagrams/fad31dc7-a3d7-5811-bda5-aa6b63c30935/del34.svg)

**Case 2: one child.** Splice the child up: the parent's pointer now points at the node's only child, then free the node. `delete(47)`, where 47 is 45's right child and 46 is its only child, is `45->right = 46; free 47`. It's `right` because **47** was a right child; which side 46 hangs on doesn't matter.

![removing 47, which has one child](courses/diagrams/9a90b498-859d-5ccd-b8f4-4179b5c56551/del47.svg)

**Case 3: two children. The class rule:** find q, the **largest key in the left subtree**: go left once, then right until there's no right child. Copy q's key into the node, then delete q.

![finding q, the largest key in 49's left subtree](courses/diagrams/6920b100-532e-5a21-9b5f-b97ffacd80b1/find_q.svg)

![copy 47 into the node](courses/diagrams/6920b100-532e-5a21-9b5f-b97ffacd80b1/copy_q.svg)

![remove the old 47 with case 2](courses/diagrams/6920b100-532e-5a21-9b5f-b97ffacd80b1/remove_q.svg)

q was found by going right until there was no right child, so q **never has a right child**. Deleting q is always case 1 or case 2. The smallest key in the right subtree (the successor) would also give a valid BST, and that tree is his usual wrong answer: use the left side unless the question says otherwise.

The whole delete walks down one path (to the node, then on to q), so it is **O(h)**: O(log n) when balanced, O(n) for a chain.

- **Hidden worst case.** "Each comparison throws away a subtree, so it's O(log n)." That only holds while the tree is balanced. Every BST operation is O(h), and h can be n − 1. Before you accept "even in the worst case", picture the chain you get from sorted inserts.
- **Local check, global rule.** "To check X, it's enough to look at each node and its children." The BST rule is about **whole subtrees**: every key on the left is smaller, every key on the right is bigger. A grandchild can break it while every parent-child pair looks fine.
- **Wrong "because".** The conclusion may be right, the reason not. Ask whether the code really does what the reason says.
- **Edge-case truths.** Statements about odd shapes, like a tree with only one kind of child. Draw a three-node example and run the traversals. These are often True.
- **Class conventions.** Two-child remove copies in the **largest key of the left subtree**; an empty tree has height −1; insert ignores duplicates.

lessons.title: Heap or Not: Shape and Order
lessons.readme:
# Heap or Not: Shape and Order

A **max-heap** is a binary tree with two rules, and the exam checks them separately.

**Rule 1, order: every parent is ≥ its children.**

![a max-heap](courses/diagrams/94bd5748-499e-5227-a4d8-961d7414b5db/max_heap.svg)

Follow that rule down from the top and the root has to be the biggest key in the whole tree. That's all the order a heap keeps. Siblings don't care about each other, so a heap is **not sorted** and is **not a BST**. The smallest key can sit in **any leaf**.

Because "≥" chains down the tree, checking each parent against its own two children is enough to prove the whole heap is ordered. Compare that with a BST, where checking only a node's children is **not** enough.

**Rule 2, shape: the tree is complete.** Every level is full except possibly the last one, and the last level fills from the **left** with no gaps.

![a complete tree next to one with a gap](courses/diagrams/94bd5748-499e-5227-a4d8-961d7414b5db/complete.svg)

The shape rule keeps the tree about log₂ n levels tall, which is why push and pop are fast.

**Worked check.** Is `[60, 45, 50, 20, 48, 10]` a max-heap? Index 1 holds 45, and its children are at 3 and 4: 20 and 48. 48 > 45, so heap order breaks there. As an array it's always complete; shape problems show up in **drawn** trees with a missing left child or a gap.

> [!warning]
> The trap is mixing up which rule broke. A node with a right child but no left child breaks **shape**, even if every parent is bigger than its children.

# Heap Index Math, 0-Based

You don't need nodes or pointers for a heap. Number the nodes level by level, left to right, and store them in an array in that order.

![a heap with its array indexes](courses/diagrams/2ed75a0d-6cc2-54ec-b6f0-b16925fec570/indexes.svg)

The tree is complete, so there are no gaps, and simple math finds any node's family. For the node at index `i`:

- left child: `2i + 1`
- right child: `2i + 2`
- parent: `(i - 1) / 2` (C++ integer division drops the remainder)

Check it on the picture. Index 1 holds 70. Its children are at 2·1 + 1 = 3 and 2·1 + 2 = 4, which hold 40 and 60. Index 6 holds 75, and its parent is (6 − 1) / 2 = 2, which holds 80.

**The last parent.** With n keys, the last index is n − 1, so the last node that has a child is its parent: `(n - 2) / 2`, which is `n/2 - 1`. Everything after it is a leaf. With n = 10 that's index 4, whose left child is 9.

> [!warning]
> Some textbooks start the root at index 1 and use `2i`, `2i + 1` and `i / 2`. This class starts at **index 0**. A question that gives you `i / 2` as the parent formula is testing whether you notice.

# Write It: Push with Sift-Up

To add a key, we have to keep both rules true.

**Shape first.** The only spot that keeps the tree complete is the next free slot: the end of the array.

**Then order.** The new key might be bigger than its parent. If it is, swap them, and keep swapping upward until its parent is bigger or it reaches the root. This is called **sift-up** (or "bubble up").

Here's `push(85)`. The key on the move is amber; the parent it's compared with is blue.

![push 85, steps 1 and 2](courses/diagrams/cd575b2c-983e-596c-8a19-1a4e0f99fa65/push_a.svg)

![push 85, steps 3 and 4](courses/diagrams/cd575b2c-983e-596c-8a19-1a4e0f99fa65/push_b.svg)

Notice that only the keys on one path, from the new leaf up to the root, ever move. Everything else stays put.

## Assignment

New students keep arriving. Write `push` so each one lands in the right place.

1. [ ] Append `key` to the end of `A`.
2. [ ] Let `i` be its index.
3. [ ] While `i > 0` and the parent's key is smaller than `A[i]`: swap them, and move `i` up to the parent.

`std::swap(a, b)` swaps two values.

lessons.readme:
# Write It: Pop with Sift-Down

The doctor is free. Who's next? That's easy: `top()` is just `A[0]`.

Removing it is the interesting part. If we simply deleted the root, the tree would have a hole at the top. Instead:

1. Move the **last** key into the root. The tree stays complete.
2. Shrink the array by one.
3. The new root is probably too small, so **sift it down**: swap it with its **larger** child, and keep going until both children are smaller or it hits a leaf.

Here's a pop from the heap we got last lesson. 90 is removed:

![pop, steps 1 and 2](courses/diagrams/037abc8a-b824-5347-b17f-25bdd7444ddd/pop_a.svg)

![pop, steps 3 and 4](courses/diagrams/037abc8a-b824-5347-b17f-25bdd7444ddd/pop_b.svg)

**Why the larger child?** Whichever child moves up becomes the parent of the other one. If we swapped 40 with 80 in step 2, 80 would end up above 85, and the order rule would break right there.

> [!note]
> In the lecture's priority queue, `pop()` returns nothing. Read `top()` first, then `pop()`. `std::priority_queue` works the same way.

## Assignment

1. [ ] Complete `siftDown(A, i, n)`. Only the first `n` elements count as the heap. Find the index of the largest of `A[i]` and its children (a child exists only if its index is `< n`). If that isn't `i`, swap and keep sifting from the child's index.
2. [ ] Complete `top(A)`.
3. [ ] Complete `pop(A)`: move the last key to the root, shrink the vector with `pop_back()`, then sift down from the root.

You can assume the heap isn't empty when `top` or `pop` is called.

lessons.readme:
# Push and Pop Traces

Both operations keep the shape rule first, then repair the order along **one path**.

**push(x):** put x at the end of the array (the next free slot keeps the tree complete). While it is bigger than its parent, swap them and move up.

**pop():** move the **last** key into the root, shrink the array by one, then sift the root down: swap it with its **larger** child until both children are smaller or it is a leaf.

Why the larger child? Whichever child moves up becomes the parent of the other one. Swap with the smaller child and the bigger one ends up below it, which breaks the order right there.

**Worked trace.** Start with `[90, 70, 80, 40, 60, 50, 75]`.

- `push(85)`: 85 lands at index 7. Its parent is index 3 (40): swap. Now at index 3, parent index 1 (70): swap. Now at index 1, parent 90 is bigger: stop. Result `[90, 85, 80, 70, 60, 50, 75, 40]`.
- `pop()`: 40 (the last key) moves to the root: `[40, 85, 80, 70, 60, 50, 75]`. Children 85 and 80, larger is 85: swap. At index 1, children 70 and 60, larger is 70: swap. Index 3 has no children: stop. Result `[85, 70, 80, 40, 60, 50, 75]`.

**Cost.** Each step is one comparison and at most one swap, and the path is about log₂ n long, so push and pop are both **O(log n)** even in the worst case. `top()` is O(1): it's `A[0]`.

> [!warning]
> The trap is "swap with the left child because the tree fills from the left". Filling from the left is the shape rule. Sift-down always picks the larger child.

lessons.title: Build-Heap in O(n)
lessons.readme:
# Build-Heap in O(n)

You start with an unordered array and want a max-heap, in place.

Every **leaf** is already a heap of one node. So skip the leaves and fix the parents: start at the **last parent**, `n/2 - 1`, and go **backward** to index 0, calling sift-down on each one.

![buildHeap, one sift-down per step from index 4 back to the root](courses/diagrams/21f066b9-67ad-5ef9-bc30-23df252a3012/start.svg)

**Why backward?** Sift-down only works if both subtrees below are already heaps. Going from the bottom up guarantees that: by the time you reach a node, everything under it has been fixed.

**Worked trace** on `[3, 9, 5, 7, 8, 1]` (n = 6, so start at index 2):

- i = 2: 5 vs its child 1. Fine.
- i = 1: 9 vs 7 and 8. Fine.
- i = 0: 3 vs 9 and 5. Swap with 9: `[9, 3, 5, 7, 8, 1]`. Keep going at index 1: 3 vs 7 and 8, swap with 8: `[9, 8, 5, 7, 3, 1]`.

**Why O(n), not O(n log n)?** A node can only sink as far as the levels below it. Half the nodes are leaves and never move, a quarter can move 1 level, an eighth 2 levels, and so on. n/4 · 1 + n/8 · 2 + n/16 · 3 + … adds up to less than n. Only the few nodes near the top can sink far.

> [!warning]
> "n/2 sift-downs at O(log n) each, so O(n log n)" is a true **upper bound** but not the tight one, and the exam wants **O(n)**. Building with n separate pushes really is O(n log n), and it can give a different array.

lessons.readme:
# Heapsort Step by Step

A max-heap always hands you the biggest remaining key. Heapsort uses that with no extra array:

1. `buildHeap` on the whole array.
2. **Swap** `A[0]` (the max) with the last key of the heap. That key is now in its final sorted spot.
3. The heap is one smaller. Sift the new root down, **within the heap part only**.
4. Repeat until the heap is one key.

![one heapsort pass, then the start of the next](courses/diagrams/f4d5d5e5-3852-5efb-a9f3-22aa94d88bbb/pass.svg)

**Worked trace** on the heap `[9, 7, 8, 3, 5, 6]`. Swap 9 and 6: `[6, 7, 8, 3, 5 | 9]`. Sift 6 down in a heap of size 5: larger child is 8, swap: `[8, 7, 6, 3, 5 | 9]`. Next pass: swap 8 and 5: `[5, 7, 6, 3 | 8, 9]`, sift 5 down: `[7, 5, 6, 3 | 8, 9]`.

> [!warning]
> The classic bug is sifting down with the **old** size. Then the sorted key at the end counts as part of the heap again and gets pulled back up.

| Step | How often | Cost |
|---|---|---|
| buildHeap | once | O(n) |
| swap + sift-down | n − 1 times | O(log n) each |
| **total** | | **O(n log n)** |

That's the same in the **best, average and worst** case. No input can make heapsort O(n²), unlike quicksort with a bad pivot. Merge sort is also always O(n log n) but needs an O(n) extra array.

**Stable?** No. The long jump from the root to the end can reorder equal keys.

**Space.** Keys only move inside the array. But the sift-down from class is **recursive**, up to log n calls deep, so as written heapsort is **O(log n)** space. The professor crossed out "O(1)" on the slides for that reason. With a loop sift-down it is O(1).

answers: It runs in O(n) when the input is already sorted

It is stable, while quicksort is not stable
Like merge sort, it needs an extra O(n) array
questions.answer: No input order can push it to O(n²), unlike quicksort

This lesson and the Choice and Code lesson copy the professor's quiz layout: five true/false here, then three multiple choice and a fill-in-the-blank C++ function in the next lesson. On his quizzes points are usually lost to the wording, not the idea. Here are the traps he builds heap questions from.

- **Real invariant.** Some plain statements are simply true. About half of his true/false items are.

lessons.readme:
# Degrees, Kₙ and Euler Walks

The **degree** of a vertex is the number of edge ends touching it. Every edge has exactly **two ends**, so adding up all the degrees counts every edge twice:

**sum of all degrees = 2E**

So degrees 3, 3, 2, 2, 4 add to 14, which means **7 edges**. It also means the sum is always even, so the number of **odd**-degree vertices is always even too.

A **complete graph** Kₙ has an edge between every pair of its n vertices. Each vertex has n − 1 neighbors, so the degrees add to n(n − 1), and every edge was counted twice:

**Kₙ has n(n − 1) / 2 edges**

![the complete graph K5, every vertex has degree 4](courses/diagrams/10a9e4d2-39a3-51ff-80bb-9b3506623360/k5.svg)

K₅ has 5 · 4 / 2 = **10**. If it's directed with arrows both ways, don't divide by 2: 20.

**Euler walks** use every edge exactly once. Each time a walk passes **through** a vertex it uses two edges, one in and one out, so odd leftovers can only be at the two ends of the walk. For a connected graph:

- **Euler circuit** (ends where it started): every vertex has **even** degree.
- **Euler path** (start ≠ end): **exactly 2** vertices have odd degree, and you must start at one of them and finish at the other.

![the Königsberg bridges as a multigraph](courses/diagrams/a5665e89-1cbc-5090-b04f-427461e9c13b/kberg.svg)

Königsberg's degrees are 5, 3, 3, 3: four odd vertices. No circuit, and not even a path.

> [!warning]
> The trap is a graph with exactly two odd vertices sold as having a **circuit**. Two odd vertices give a path only.

# Reading Matrices and Lists

Two ways to store a graph, and one rule to read both: **`A[i][j] = 1` means an edge i → j.**

![a directed graph and its matrix, row 2 highlighted](courses/diagrams/d2ddcd33-c3de-5b46-a6cb-f209fcdcdc73/dir.svg)

- **Row i** lists i's **out**-neighbors. **Column j** lists who points **into** j.
- An **undirected** edge sets both `A[u][v]` and `A[v][u]`, so the matrix is **symmetric**. A directed matrix is not necessarily symmetric.
- An **adjacency list** keeps one list per vertex. An undirected edge appears in **two** lists (2E entries in total); a directed edge appears only in its tail's list (E entries).

To read a list off a matrix, go along the row and write down the column number of every 1. Row 2 above is `1 0 0 1`, so `2 → 0, 3`.

| | Matrix | List |
|---|---|---|
| space | O(V²) | O(V + E) |
| "is (u, v) an edge?" | O(1) | O(degree of u): scan u's list |
| all neighbors of u | O(V): the whole row | O(degree of u) |
| best when | dense, small V, many edge checks | sparse, visit every neighbor |

Most real graphs (roads, social networks) are sparse, so lists are the usual default.

> [!warning]
> The swapped-pair trap: "O(1) edge check" belongs to the **matrix**, and "O(V + E) space" belongs to the **list**. Another trap is reading a column when the question asks where a vertex's edges **go**.

# Write It: Recursive DFS Order

Now we can store the campus. Next question: starting from one building, which spots can you reach at all? That's a **traversal**: visit every vertex reachable from a start vertex, **exactly once**.

On a tree, recursion alone works, because there's only one path to each node. A graph can have **cycles** (A → B → E → F → C → A below), and plain recursion would go around one forever. So we keep a `visited[]` array and skip anything already marked.

**Depth-first search** goes deep: follow one path until you're stuck, then back up and try the next branch, like exploring a maze.

```cpp
dfs(v):
    visited[v] = true
    visit(v)                      // e.g. print v
    for each neighbor w of v
        if not visited[w]
            dfs(w)
```

DFS is naturally recursive: `dfs(w)` runs to completion before v tries its next neighbor. The call stack is DFS's stack. Here's `dfs(A)`, neighbors in alphabetical order:

![DFS steps 1 and 2](courses/diagrams/6c978319-cca8-53a8-a69a-a21156f79e74/s1.svg)

![DFS steps 3 and 4](courses/diagrams/6c978319-cca8-53a8-a69a-a21156f79e74/s2.svg)

The final visit order is **A B D E F C G**. Edge A–C (blue in step 3) is never followed, because C was already visited when A got around to it. The green edges form the **DFS tree**.

## Assignment

1. [ ] Complete `dfs(adj, v, visited, order)`: mark v, append it to `order`, then recurse on each unvisited neighbor **in list order**.
2. [ ] Complete `dfsOrder(adj, s)`: make a `visited` vector (all false) and an empty `order`, call `dfs` from `s` once, and return `order`. Only the vertices reachable from `s` appear.

# Write It: BFS Order with a Queue

DFS charges down one path. For directions we'd rather explore outward evenly: everything 1 walkway away, then 2, then 3, like a ripple in a pond. That's **breadth-first search**, and the tool that keeps the rings in order is a **queue**.

```cpp
bfs(s):
    queue q
    visited[s] = true
    q.push(s)
    while q is not empty
        v = q.front()
        q.pop()
        visit(v)
        for each neighbor w of v
            if not visited[w]
                visited[w] = true
                q.push(w)
```

The queue is first in, first out, so every vertex at distance k leaves the queue before any vertex at distance k + 1. Here's BFS from A on the graph from the DFS lesson:

![BFS steps 1 and 2](courses/diagrams/6c22ab0e-3501-543e-aead-ee8db83fd61c/b1.svg)

![BFS steps 3 and 4](courses/diagrams/6c22ab0e-3501-543e-aead-ee8db83fd61c/b2.svg)

Popping D adds nothing. Popping E adds G, and then F and G add nothing new. The visit order is **A B C D E F G**.

> [!warning]
> Mark a vertex **when you push it**, not when you pop it. If you wait until the pop, a vertex can be pushed twice: in the picture, F is a neighbor of both C and E.

## Assignment

1. [ ] Complete `bfsOrder(adj, s)`: return the vertices reachable from `s` in BFS visit order, trying neighbors in list order. Use `std::queue<int>` (`push`, `front`, `pop`, `empty`).

lessons.readme:
# DFS and BFS Orders on Paper

The exam hands you a graph and asks for the visit order, with neighbors tried in increasing order. Write the adjacency lists first, then trace.

**DFS uses a stack (the recursion).** Visit the start. At the top call, scan its list from **where you left off** for the first unvisited neighbor; visit it and push. If none is left, pop back to the **caller**, which carries on scanning **its** list.

**BFS uses a queue.** Start with `[s]`, s marked. Pop the front, go through its list, and mark and push every unmarked neighbor. Mark a vertex **when you push it**, not when you pop it, or it can be pushed twice.

**Worked example.** Edges 0–1, 0–2, 1–3, 2–3, 2–4, 3–5, 4–5:

```
0: 1 2      3: 1 2 5
1: 0 3      4: 2 5
2: 0 3 4    5: 3 4
```

- DFS from 0: 0 → 1 → 3 (1's next) → 2 (3's next unvisited) → 4 → 5. Order **0 1 3 2 4 5**.
- BFS from 0: pop 0, push 1 2. Pop 1, push 3. Pop 2, push 4. Pop 3, push 5. Pop 4, pop 5. Order **0 1 2 3 4 5**.

**Cost.** With adjacency lists each vertex is visited once and each list is scanned once: **O(V + E)** for both. With a matrix, finding one vertex's neighbors scans a whole row, so both are **O(V²)**.

**DFS on a binary tree**, left child first, visits a node, then goes deep left, then right. That's **pre-order**.

> [!warning]
> The usual DFS mistake is jumping to the next vertex in number order after a dead end, instead of returning to the caller.

# Dijkstra by Hand

**Dijkstra's algorithm** finds the shortest distance from s to every vertex when every edge weight is ≥ 0. Each vertex is either **finished** (its distance is final) or **unfinished** (best found so far).

Start with `dist[s] = 0` and every other `dist` at ∞. Then repeat:

1. **Finish** the unfinished vertex u with the smallest `dist`.
2. **Relax** each edge (u, v): if `dist[u] + len < dist[v]`, lower `dist[v]` and set `prev[v] = u`.

![Dijkstra steps 1 and 2](courses/diagrams/e6c1cace-3aab-5259-be75-c61fc444f908/d1.svg)

![Dijkstra steps 3 and 4](courses/diagrams/e6c1cace-3aab-5259-be75-c61fc444f908/d2.svg)

![Dijkstra steps 5 and 6](courses/diagrams/e6c1cace-3aab-5259-be75-c61fc444f908/d3.svg)

In step 3, relaxing P–S lowers S from 120 to 100. A distance can keep improving until its vertex is finished.

**On paper**, keep one table with a column per vertex and a row per step:

| finish | MH | P | S | F | R | EC |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| MH 0 | **0** | 60 | 120 | ∞ | 300 | ∞ |
| P 60 | | **60** | 100 | 210 | 300 | ∞ |
| S 100 | | | **100** | 170 | 220 | ∞ |
| F 170 | | | | **170** | 220 | 210 |
| EC 210 | | | | | 220 | **210** |

**Rebuilding the route.** `prev[v]` is the vertex right before v. Start at the target and follow `prev` back to the source, then **reverse**: EC ← F ← S ← P ← MH gives MH → P → S → F → EC.

> [!warning]
> The trap in a trace is finishing vertices in the order you first **saw** them (that's BFS). Always finish the smallest `dist` that isn't finished yet, even if it was just lowered.

lessons.readme:
# Dijkstra's Fine Print

**It's greedy.** Each step finishes the closest unfinished vertex and never revisits that choice. That's safe because any other route to it would have to leave the finished set through an unfinished vertex that already costs at least as much, and edges ≥ 0 can't make a route cheaper.

**It breaks with negative edges**, even with no negative cycle:

![a directed graph with one negative edge](courses/diagrams/10180abb-0fea-52a9-a31f-9c1b4497e3b8/neg.svg)

Edges s → a 2, s → b 3, a → c 4, b → a −2. Dijkstra finishes a at 2 and sets c = 6. Then b → a would lower a to 1, but a is already finished, so c stays **6**. The real shortest is s → b → a → c = **5**.

**It's BFS with a min-heap.** Swap BFS's FIFO queue for a **min-heap** of `{dist, v}` pairs: closest first, not oldest first. When a distance improves, push a new pair; when a stale pair comes out later, its vertex is already finished, so skip it.

**BFS is not Dijkstra.** BFS finds the path with the **fewest edges**. On the campus map BFS returns MH → R → EC, 2 edges but 350 m, while the shortest walk is 4 edges and 210 m.

![the campus map: the BFS route next to the shortest route](courses/diagrams/016207b8-71d1-5228-8556-f0e652bd12ad/bfs.svg)

**Big O** with adjacency lists and a binary heap: each edge is relaxed at most once per direction, and each heap push or pop is O(log V). The total is **O((V + E) log V)**. (The lazy-deletion version counts out to O(V + E log V), which fits inside that bound.)

lessons.title: When DP Applies
lessons.readme:
# When DP Applies

DP and greedy are **quiz-style only** on the final: T/F and MC, no code. Know the ideas and be able to trace them.

**Dynamic programming** means solving each distinct subproblem **once** and storing its answer so it gets reused instead of recomputed. The lecture lists what a problem needs for that to work:

1. **Optimal substructure.** A best solution is built from best solutions to smaller subproblems. The best way to cut an 8-foot board is one first piece plus the best way to cut what's left.
2. **Overlapping subproblems.** A plain recursive solution solves the same subproblems again and again.
3. **Usually an optimization problem**, a min or a max. There may be several best solutions, and DP hands back one of them.

Here's the overlap in plain recursive Fibonacci (f(0) = f(1) = 1). Red is the same work done again:

![the recursion tree of fibonacci(5), with repeated calls in red](courses/diagrams/e0cad926-722e-5c91-977d-57c654ba6337/fib5.svg)

Fifteen calls for only six different subproblems, f0 through f5. Storing each answer the first time is what saves the work.

> [!warning]
> The trap is calling every divide-and-conquer algorithm DP. Merge sort splits into smaller problems too, but its two halves **never overlap**, so there's nothing worth storing. That's plain divide and conquer.

lessons.title: Fibonacci Three Ways
lessons.readme:
# Fibonacci Three Ways

**Plain recursion** calls fib(n − 1) and fib(n − 2) every time. The call tree almost doubles each level: 15 calls for fib(5), 25 for fib(6). That's **O(2ⁿ)**.

**Top-down (memoization)** is the same recursion plus a cache. Base case first; then if n is in the cache, return the stored answer; otherwise compute it, **save it**, and return it.

![the call tree of memoized fib(5): 9 calls, two of them cache hits](courses/diagrams/a21ef050-0e40-51f5-b268-8acab1bd98bb/memo5.svg)

Each fib(k) is computed once and every computed value makes at most two calls, so the run makes about **2n − 1** calls: 9 for fib(5), 11 for fib(6). Time **O(n)**, space O(n) for the cache plus the call stack.

**Bottom-up (a table)** starts from the smallest subproblems and fills upward with a loop, so every value it needs is already there:

![filling f[2] and f[3]](courses/diagrams/9022d233-a82a-58b8-bd9d-dd55c53b4d2f/fill_a.svg)

Also O(n) time and O(n) space, but there's **no call stack**, so a big n can't overflow it.

| | Top-down | Bottom-up |
|---|---|---|
| shape | recursion + cache | loop filling a table |
| starts at | fib(n) | f[0], f[1] |
| solves | only the subproblems it reaches | every subproblem up to n |

> [!warning]
> Memoization **is** DP, the top-down kind. Both count because both solve each subproblem once and store it. "Memoization isn't DP because it still recurses" is a false "because".

lessons.readme:
# Rod Cutting by the Recurrence

A board n feet long sells for `price[len]` per piece, and cuts fall on whole feet. How should you cut it to earn the most?

**Brute force is exponential.** An n-foot board has n − 1 marks, and each is cut or not, so there are **2ⁿ⁻¹** ways. A 4-foot board has 8:

![all eight ways to cut a 4-foot board](courses/diagrams/4ed3c1f1-630f-5259-b977-410775e12627/four_foot.svg)

**The recurrence.** Every cut has some **first piece** of length i (i = j means selling it whole). What's left is a (j − i)-foot board, and you want the best for it:

**best[0] = 0**
**best[j] = max over i = 1..j of ( price[i] + best[j − i] )**

Fill it bottom-up from 0 feet. The amber cell is being filled; the blue cells are the `best[j − i]` values it reads:

![best[3] and best[4]](courses/diagrams/b9337211-ae09-5de5-8241-89cf4f79d45d/rod_b.svg)

**Worked example** with prices 1, 6, 10, 12 for lengths 1 to 4: best[1] = 1, best[2] = max(1 + 1, 6) = 6, best[3] = max(1 + 6, 6 + 1, 10) = 10, best[4] = max(1 + 10, 6 + 6, 10 + 1, 12) = 12.

**Cost.** Length j tries j first pieces, so 1 + 2 + … + n = n(n + 1)/2 tries: **O(n²)** time and O(n) space, compared with O(2ⁿ) for trying every cut.

Prices for lengths 1, 2, 3, 4 are 2, 5, 7, 9. Using the rod cutting recurrence, what is best[4]?
Bottom-up rod cutting is O(n²), because length j tries j different first pieces.
Trying every possible cut of an n-foot rod is O(n²), the same as the DP table.

lessons.title: Greedy: Fast, Final, Sometimes Wrong
lessons.readme:
# Greedy: Fast, Final, Sometimes Wrong

A **greedy algorithm** takes the option that looks best **right now** and never goes back to reconsider it. No table, no trying alternatives, so it's simple and fast.

**Coin change, biggest coin first.** For 65 cents with US coins (25, 10, 5, 1):

![greedy change for 65 cents: 25, 25, 10, 5](courses/diagrams/fa76f884-ea80-50bd-b7d5-aeee8b398ab9/us65.svg)

For US coins this always gives the fewest coins. **Dijkstra** is greedy too: it finishes the closest vertex and never revisits it, which is safe when edges are ≥ 0.

**When greedy fails.** With tokens 1, 3 and 4 and an amount of 6, greedy grabs the 4 and is left with 2, which costs two 1s:

![greedy gives 4+1+1 but 3+3 uses fewer tokens](courses/diagrams/f2e07ce3-79f8-53e5-8e68-263a67ccd13d/tokens6.svg)

Three tokens, when 3 + 3 uses two. The best answer doesn't have to start with the biggest coin, so DP tries every coin as the first one: **best[a] = min over coins c ≤ a of (1 + best[a − c])**. One counterexample is enough to show greedy fails; try amounts just above the biggest coin.

**Greedy can work with the right rule.** To fit the most meetings in one room, always take the request that **finishes** earliest among those that still fit. Taking the one that **starts** earliest can grab a long meeting and fit fewer.

> [!warning]
> "Greedy coin change is optimal" is only true for some coin systems. A statement with "for any coins" is the trap.
